10898-american-scenes-and-christian-slav:
Ebenezer Davies, a minister lately of Berbice in Guiana, toured more than four thousand miles of the United States in the 1840s and published this account in 1849. Entering at New Orleans, he travelled north to Boston and west to Utica, watching slavery at close hand as a British abolitionist and a pastor whose own congregation included formerly enslaved people.

Davies describes Southern plantations, Northern churches, and the growth of Puritan principles in New England, praising what he admires and denouncing what he finds cruel. He also notes American expansion and the talk of annexation. The book gives a foreign visitor's view of the republic on the eve of its great sectional crisis, sharp on slavery and curious about everything else.
10989-our-saviour:
Father Tuck's New Testament series presents the life of Jesus for children in this short illustrated book. The story begins at Nazareth, where Jesus lives quietly until John the Baptist preaches and baptises in the Jordan. John says one greater will come, then baptises Jesus himself, despite feeling unworthy, and the Spirit descends like a dove as a voice calls Jesus the beloved Son.

Forty days of temptation in the wilderness follow, then preaching by the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus calls fishermen as disciples. Later scenes show special kindness to little children, whom the disciples would turn away, and a child set among disputing disciples to teach humility. Simple language and pictures make the Gospel story accessible to young readers.
11085-m-or-n-similia-similibus-curantur:
G. J. Whyte-Melville wrote this Victorian novel of society, crime, and love, titled M. or N. and subtitled Similia similibus curantur, like cures like. A wild wet night in the Channel opens the story, with cross-seas off Calais, a French sentry humming opera, and a Queen's Messenger sick on the mail packet. Tom Ryfe, Gentleman Jim, Dick Stanmore, and Nina carry the plot through thirty chapters.

Cracksmen, officers' messes, missing gentlemen and wanted ladies, and a coming queen mix with balls, tea-rooms, and partings. Dick watches a lady with another man in a deserted tea-room and knows his first misfortune has come. Whyte-Melville, known for hunting novels, writes here a tale of London and country society, with rogues and lovers crossing paths.
11266-sonnets-by-the-nawab-nizamat-jung-:
This 1917 sonnet sequence by the Nawab Nizamat Jung Bahadur, privately printed in Madras in 1914, gathers twenty-four sonnets on love in its highest sense. from Rebirth and Before the Throne through Love's Silence, Eternal Joy, and Two Hearts in One, with a prologue and epilogue. Epigraphs from Empedocles and Plato frame love as nourishment for the soul's wings. A foreword by R. C. Fraser introduces the author.

Born in Hyderabad and educated in England, the Nawab wrote during rare leisure in a busy public life, and Fraser notes his popular war lyric India to England. A note on the sonnet's history in English literature accompanies the poems. The volume offers a distinctive meeting of Indian devotion and English form.
12588-cavour:
Countess Evelyn Martinengo-Cesaresco's 1898 life of Cavour traces the statesman who made modern Italy. Chapters move from heredity and environment through travel years, journalism and parliament to the great ministry. The Crimean War, the Congress of Paris, the pact of Plombières, the war of 1859, Savoy and Nice, the Sicilian expedition and the kingdom of Italy follow.

Cavour, the book argues, worked by evolution, not catastrophe, though change often looks like leaps and bounds. Rome voted capital closes the story. Martinengo-Cesaresco writes as an admiring biographer, clear on diplomacy and character. The life remains a readable English portrait of Italian unification, centred on its ablest minister.
13193-supreme-personality-fun-in-living-:
Dr. Delmer Eugene Croft's Supreme Personality, subtitled Fun in Living, is a twenty-five-cent cure for doubt, fear, and worry, in its hundredth thousand printing. Croft promises that a reader can grow grander and handsomer at eighty than at eighteen, if the spiritual, mental, and physical cash register stays in order. Thought waves, he claims, can heal, guide, and build personal power.

Pages give exercises for breath and muscle, urging deep abdominal breaths through the nose and forceful release through the mouth, never holding the breath. Croft cites Vanderbilt adding millions after eighty, Wordsworth winning the laureateship at seventy-three, and Verdi writing Falstaff late in life. The booklet is cheerful, brash self-help from the age of mind power.
13433-a-reply-to-dr-lightfoot-s-essays-b:
Walter R. Cassels, writing anonymously in 1889 as the author of Supernatural Religion, answers Bishop Lightfoot's essays on his work. He opens by welcoming Lightfoot's recovery from illness, then turns to the hard question at issue: whether early Christian writings can be shown genuine, and what their silence proves.

Cassels argues that epistles whose authenticity is so hard to establish cannot carry great weight, and he tests claims that Polycarp quotes the Gospels. Point by point, footnote by footnote, he states the case for sceptics in its strongest form before answering it. The book is a dense Victorian debate over dates, texts, and the roots of Christian belief.
14072-primitive-christian-worship-or-the:
J. Endell Tyler, rector of Saint Giles-in-the-Fields, published this second edition in 1847 against the invocation of saints, angels, and the Virgin Mary. Scripture and church history supply his evidence, and his preface pleads for less hostility between Roman Catholics and Anglicans. Prove all things and hold fast what is good stands as his motto.

Close reading carries the case. Tyler tests patristic quotations, exposing one prayer wrongly credited to Origen on the Lamentations. He then turns to Luke, where the boy Jesus tells his parents he must be about his Father's business, and to the wedding at Cana. Neither passage, he argues, grants Mary divine honor. Long, learned, and partisan, the book remains a clear record of Victorian church controversy fought with footnotes.
14878-the-relation-of-the-hro-lfs-saga-k:
Oscar Ludvig Olson's 1916 dissertation, submitted to the University of Chicago for a doctorate in English, studies the relation of Hrolfs Saga Kraka and the Bjarkarimur to Beowulf. It is a contribution to the history of saga development in England and the Scandinavian countries.

Bibliography and abbreviations open the work, with line numbers following A. J. Wyatt's edition of Beowulf and references to journals of Nordic philology and history. Olson traces shared heroes, plots and motifs across Old English and Old Norse texts. The private edition, distributed by Chicago libraries, remains a scholarly source for readers tracing Beowulf's northern kin.
15148-six-feet-four:
Jackson Gregory's 1917 Western opens in a mountain storm that snaps tall pines and darkens the canyons by midday. Chapters follow Buck Thornton, a man's man, through a ford, a ranch on Big Little River, and a dance at Deer Creek schoolhouse. Rattlesnake Pollard, the Bedloe boys, and a frame-up raise the stakes.

Winifred judges a man, Jimmie squares himself, and a showdown looms as a gentleman from New Mexico enters the game. Gregory writes in the pulp Western style, with action, romance, and frontier justice. Fans of classic Westerns will enjoy the storm, the ranch feuds, and the tall hero of the title.
15563-reason-and-faith-their-claims-and-:
Henry Rogers wrote this review essay for the Edinburgh Review of October 1849, pages 293 to 356, on reason and faith, their claims and conflicts. It reviews three books: Whately's Historic Doubts on Napoleon, Froude's Nemesis of Faith, and Foxton's Popular Christianity. The essay opens with an old divine's image: reason and faith as the patriarch's two sons, reason firstborn, faith inheriting the blessing.

Rogers calls that image ingenious but unjust. Human beings trust and believe long before they reason or know, he argues, and both powers are coeval with human nature, meant to dwell together and complete each other. The essay then tests rationalist readings of scripture, asking on what ground parts of a record can be rejected as improbable. It is a learned Victorian defense of faith that still reasons, not a plea for blind belief.
16327-at-home-and-abroad-or-things-and-t:
Margaret Fuller Ossoli gathers travel writing from both sides of the Atlantic in this 1869 volume, edited by her brother Arthur. Summer on the Lakes opens the book, with notes on the American West, its people, and its promise. Letters from Europe and a homeward voyage follow, with memorial pieces at the end.

Fuller writes as a keen observer who judges what she sees, not a tourist listing sights. Her preface sorts travelers into those who see nothing and those who learn, and she plainly aims to be among the learners. The book gives a mid-century American mind meeting Europe, and it still reads fresh and sharp.
16538-the-alleged-haunting-of-b-house-in:
A. Goodrich-Freer and the Marquess of Bute edited this 1899 inquiry into the alleged haunting of B House, with a journal kept during Colonel Lemesurier Taylor's tenancy. Lord Bute first heard of the case in 1892, and the book sets out the claims, the plans of attics and floors, and the evidence as the investigators found it.

The Society for Psychical Research declined to print the inquiry in its Proceedings, a fact the editors quote from the Times of June 1897. The book therefore reads as both ghost story and cold case file. Readers of hauntings will find it careful, curious, and unresolved in the best way.
16677-the-chink-in-the-armour:
Mrs. Belloc Lowndes wrote this 1912 tale of Paris, crime, and society, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York. Sylvia Bailey, staying at the Hotel de l'Horloge, finds a small pink card from Madame Cagliostra, fortune teller of Montmartre, among cards from dressmakers and hairdressers. The card draws her toward a world of seers and danger.

Lowndes builds dread from small signs: a card, a visit, a hint of murder in a polite world that assumes murder will not happen. The title points to that weak spot in civil life. Readers who like quiet thrillers will enjoy its Paris setting, its social detail, and its slow tightening of fear around one young woman.
16957-mr-sponge-s-sporting-tour:
R. S. Surtees wrote this sporting novel of Mr. Sponge, dedicated to Lord Elcho for many seasons of excellent sport with his hounds on the border. It opens on a murky October day, as Sponge, called Soapey by his friends, mizzles along Oxford Street toward the West. His daily round runs from the Bantam Hotel through Piccadilly and Leicester Square to Aldridge's and Moore's sporting print shop.

Surtees follows Sponge through hunts, horse deals, and country houses, with satire aimed at sporting folk and their manners. The humor is rough, social, and full of horse talk. Readers who like Victorian sporting novels will find a comic, episodic tour, best read for its characters and its skewering of hunt society.
17095-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-on-:
In Laura Lee Hope's 1917 tale, Bunny Brown and Sue set out on a motor tour with their family and their dog. A boy next door, a lost dog named Dix, a flood, a fire, a medicine show, and a loose lion at the circus crowd the road. Camping, lake stops, and a ditch mishap keep the trip lively from town to town.

The charm is in small, kind deeds: the children help strangers, chase lost pets, and face each scare with pluck. Short chapters and homely talk make the book easy for young readers. It stands as a sunny road story from the early age of cars, when a family auto trip still felt like a grand event.
17520-letters-of-the-right-honourable-la:
Lady Mary Wortley Montagu's letters were written during her travels in Europe, Asia, and Africa. They went to persons of distinction and men of letters in different parts of Europe. This new edition, complete in one volume, was printed in London in 1790 for Thomas Martin. The letters promise accounts of the policy and manners of the Turks, drawn from sources inaccessible to other travellers.

A preface by a lady, written in 1724, introduces the collection, noting that the letters were not meant for common editors' advertisement. Readers get one of the great travel letter collections in English, witty, observant, and famously frank about Turkish life. The book suits readers of travel writing and of eighteenth-century women writers.
17626-the-lost-gospel-and-its-contents-o:
M. F. Sadler, rector of Honiton, wrote this reply to the author of Supernatural Religion, published in London in 1876 by George Bell and Sons. Sadler explains in his preface that his book is called The Lost Gospel because the work it answers tries to discredit the supernatural element of Christianity by appeal to a lost gospel. His answer refutes the author by his own admissions.

Readers get a Victorian apologetic work, learned, combative, and closely argued. The book suits readers of biblical criticism, of Sadler's churchmanship, and of the debate over Supernatural Religion. Its interest lies in a controversy now largely forgotten.
17683-the-prairie-farmer-vol-56-no-2-jan:
Prairie Farmer, a weekly journal for the farm, orchard, and fireside, issued this number in Chicago on Saturday, January 12, 1884, as volume fifty-six, number two. The paper had been established in 1841 and cost two dollars a year in advance. Its contents page, moved to the front for ease of use, opens with agriculture, including dew and soil moisture, specialty in farming, and public squares in small cities.

Farm names and other farm notes follow in the same practical spirit. As a single weekly issue, the paper mixes farming advice with household reading for prairie families. Readers get a direct look at Midwestern farm life in the 1880s, through the paper that served it week by week.
1822-the-amateur:
Richard Harding Davis sets this sea story in February off the Banks, where the weather is so thick that on the upper decks one could have driven a sleigh. Inside the smoking-room, Austin Ford shelters from the blizzard. He listens to talk of Harry, a fellow passenger who is at meals three times a day and on deck all the rest of the day.

The amateur of the title is a man out of his depth. The story turns on what happens when a landsman tries the sea's work. Davis, who knew ships and sailors, writes the cold, the fog, and the talk of the smoking-room with care. The tale's tension comes from a simple question: can a gentleman passenger become a seaman when it matters.
19204-lady-larkspur:
Meredith Nicholson wrote this 1919 novel about a vanished actress and a roaming widow. Searles gave a year to a play meant for an actress who had vanished. Talk turns to a widow who married Uncle Bash at the American Embassy. She then travelled the Orient marrying and burying husbands. Bangkok seems absurdly remote for such a chase.

Torrence knows only official reports of Uncle Bash's death at Tokyo. He knows fussy life insurance proofs too. The house at Barton awaits a possible return. Pursuing knights, a fan, and a girl named Alice fill the chapters. Readers get a light, witty novel of society, travel, and romantic pursuit.
19441-my-friend-the-chauffeur:
C. N. Williamson and A. M. Williamson wrote this motor romance, under a New York imprint in the early nineteen hundreds with pictures by Frederic Lowenheim. Five narrators take turns telling the tale: Ralph Moray, Beechy Kidder, a countess, Maida Destrey, and Terence Barrymore.

Cars speed along the Riviera toward Alessandria and Cuneo, under skies that turn clouds to rose and silver at sunset. Surprises, plans, revenges, and predicaments follow in quick order, making the book a light, fast tour of love and motoring in southern Europe. Beechy Kidder's chapters run from playing dolls to brakes and worms, keeping the motor tour full of small mishaps.
19452-le-petit-nord-or-annals-of-a-labra:
Anne Grenfell and Katie Spalding wrote these annals of a Labrador harbour, published in the early nineteen twenties. The entries read like a household diary. Supper spoiled when a dish left in a hot oven turns to an uneatable lump, dogs in trouble, and the small trials of a remote station fill the pages.

Humor softens the hardship, as the writers joke about sanctified starvation slimming a fine figure. The book gives a rare, close view of daily life on the Labrador coast, told by women who lived it rather than visited it.
1976-peter-ruff-and-the-double-four:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's Peter Ruff and the Double Four introduces Mr. Peter Ruff. He leaves a respectable life to become a private agent for those who cannot go to the police. The contents run from Introducing Mr. Peter Ruff through Vincent Cawdor, commission agent, to Delilah from Streatham and the little lady from the country.

A scene in which a woman protests that Count von Hern has not been found, and that she saw him dancing with a tall girl in yellow, shows Oppenheim's method. The method uses a ballroom, a secret, and a hero who sees what others miss. The book gathers Ruff's cases into a single volume, and it remains a polished sample of the Edwardian adventure story.
19951-ted-strong-in-montana-or-with-lari:
Edward C. Taylor wrote the Ted Strong books, boys' westerns under the Rough Rider banner. Ted Strong in Montana opens with hard luck on the trail. High water at Poplar Fork has delayed the outfit a week. Had they left earlier, Ted says, they'd be settled at the ranch for winter. Lariat and spur, the subtitle promises, will settle things instead. Snow and rivers set the terms in Montana.

Ted Strong led his Rough Riders through many volumes of adventure. Taylor's West is work first: cattle, weather, and distance. Boys learned ranch craft between the stampedes. Montana gives this volume big country and hard winters. The series rivaled the era's other western franchises. It shows the boys' western at full gallop.
20534-a-sermon-preached-at-the-quaker-s-:
Preached at the Quakers' meeting house in Gracechurch Street, London, this sermon addresses a painful split inside the Society of Friends. The preacher speaks while proceedings in the Society are stirring strong feeling. He knows his words will be read as taking a side.

He states most plainly that the publication is no party act. It does not spring from party feeling, he says, though he must take a heartfelt interest in the matter. He feels deeply that even a friend of the cause must speak with care. The sermon preserves one voice from a forgotten Quaker quarrel.
2097-the-sign-of-the-four:
Arthur Conan Doyle's second Sherlock Holmes novel opens with Holmes at his syringe, then plunges into the case of Mary Morstan and a treasure from India. A bald-headed man, a tragedy at Pondicherry Lodge, and the Baker Street Irregulars follow. Doyle wrote The Sign of the Four in 1890, as the second Holmes novel after A Study in Scarlet.

Holmes and Watson track Jonathan Small and the Agra treasure down the Thames, and Small's strange story explains the crime. The book sets the Holmes pattern: deduction, chase, and a long confession that ties the threads together. The Agra treasure links London crime to Indian mutiny history, a link Doyle uses with care.
22259-the-legacy-of-greece-essays-by-gil:
Gilbert Murray edited The Legacy of Greece in 1921, gathering essays by leading British scholars. Murray himself, Oxford's professor of Greek, opens the volume with a challenge. If man's life were measured in dollars, miles, and horse-power, he writes, Greece must count as a poverty-stricken minute territory. Its engines stood nearer the spear and bow than the telegraph and aeroplane.

Yet Greece, the essays argue, founded Europe's reason, art, politics, and science. W. R. Inge writes on religion, J. Burnet on philosophy, and others on literature, art, and thought. The Legacy series shaped how Britain taught its civilisational debts. This first volume is its confident manifesto for the classics.
23091-the-troubadour:
Peter Michael Sherman packs a party with talk in The Troubadour. The narrator's attention wanders from the Kutrov-Alva variations, since Bill has been speaking for ten minutes and cannot be expected to arrive at any point for at least another fifteen. From the east come apocalyptic figures of nuclear physics. From the west, Mondrian interwoven with Picasso. From the south side of the room comes a dissection of the newest betrayal of popular hopes. Northward, the mysteries of atonality.

That compass of chatter maps a whole intellectual generation at one gathering. Sherman's troubadour sings among people who argue art, politics, and physics as party games. The piece belongs to the little-magazine world of clever talk. Its pleasure is eavesdropping, catching a vanished salon mid-buzz, ideologies and all.
24315-the-silesian-horseherd-questions-o:
Friedrich Max Muller, translated by Oscar A. Fechter with a foreword by J. Estlin Carpenter, published this book with Longmans, Green, and Company in 1903. Its essays answer questions of the hour, written first for a Silesian horseherd and published in the Deutsche Rundschau. Muller received many anonymous letters, but this writer's abrupt, pure, human tone appealed to him, and at leisure he attempted an answer.

The letter followed Muller's article on the True History of Celsus, in July 1895. That piece itself followed his March article on the Parliament of Religions in Chicago, which he called the most important event of 1893. Muller had named the discovery of Celsus's Sermo Verus as his most desired find. Readers get a great scholar answering a plain man's questions, in earnest and courtesy.
24535-the-path-to-honour:
Sydney C. Grier published this novel with William Blackwood and Sons at Edinburgh and London in 1909. It belongs to her long shelf of Eastern and Indian tales. Its Indian setting brings a zenana, a lavish prince named Partab Singh, soldiers, merchants, and questions of honour that can end in massacre or in death by one's own hand.

At its centre stands Gerrard, who finds that a rival's accidental death leaves honour out of his reach. Profiting from the accident would shame him as much as murder. Grier's novel mixes romance, duty, and Eastern colour into a thoughtful story of conscience.
24884-commercial-geography-a-book-for-hi:
Jacques W. Redway wrote Commercial Geography for high schools, commercial courses, and business colleges, copyrighted in 1903 and issued by Scribner in 1907. The book teaches how trade civilized mankind, then shows how land, climate, and transport shape where goods grow and go.

Chapters take up cereals, textile fibres, coal and petroleum, sugar, forests, and sea products, with a full survey of the United States. A passage on oil notes Standard Oil's reach and the Baku field on the Caspian, where output neared world markets by tank steamer and caravan. The book remains a clear picture of world trade as schools taught it in 1907.
25424-in-the-mayor-s-parlour:
J. S. Fletcher sets a murder puzzle in the market town of Hathelsborough. Its market-place, parish church, and medieval Moot Hall frame a case that turns on a cambric handkerchief, a tannery house, and nineteen missing minutes. Brent, a central figure, dreads questions at the inquest about letters he fetched from a dead man's rooms. A woman begs him to keep their heavy correspondence secret from the town.

Fletcher builds his plot from coroners, voluntary witnesses, and circumstantial evidence, with chapters on panels, castle walls, and a parlour-maid. The second edition came from John Lane, The Bodley Head, in 1922. Readers who like a slow, town-bound mystery will find its clues laid out with care.
25652-a-treasury-of-heroes-and-heroines-:
Clayton Edwards, author of The Story of Evangeline, compiles this treasury of heroes and heroines. It is a record of high endeavour and strange adventure from five hundred years before Christ to 1920, illustrated in colour by Florence Choate and Elizabeth Curtis. Cupples and Leon published it in New York in 1920.

Buddha, about five hundred years before Christ, opens the chapters. Jeanne d'Arc, drawing an arrow from her breast with a veteran's courage, fronts the book. Heroes and heroines across ages and lands fill later pages, each life told as an example of courage, endurance, and noble action for young readers.
26340-of-natural-and-supernatural-things:
Basilius Valentinus, a Benedictine monk, sets out in this 1671 London volume, translated from High Dutch by Daniel Cable, the first tincture, root, and spirit of metals and minerals. Valentinus divides all things in two: the natural, visible and tangible with form, and the supernatural, spiritual and without form, grasped by faith, not reason. Metals, he says, are first conceived in spirit, then born in body.

Added pieces treat Friar Roger Bacon on the medicine of antimony, John Isaac Holland on Saturn, and Alexander van Suchten on antimony's secrets. Mid-book claims praise a spirit of gold as a cure for leprosy, dropsy, and open sores, and as a strengthener of heart, brain, and memory. The book reads as alchemy in full voice, with its cures stated as its author's claims.
27338-baseball-joe-around-the-world-or-p:
Lester Chadwick published this boys' baseball novel with Cupples and Leon in New York in 1918. It was the eighth title in the Baseball Joe series, after books that took Joe from the school nine to Yale and the big league. Now the young pitcher sets out on a grand tour, and the game travels with him around the globe.

Chapters promise deadly peril, a gathering of the clans, rival teams, a weird game, a bewildered umpire, and even a man overboard. Joe's pitching carries the adventure from stop to stop, with close calls and hard-fought contests throughout. Young readers who follow sports stories will find the familiar hero in his widest setting yet.
27554-the-twelfth-hour:
Ada Leverson published this society novel with Chapman and Hall in London, originally in 1907 with Grant Richards and reissued in 1951. Its chapters follow Felicity, Savile, and their circle through trials, love scenes, dinners, and parties.

The book opens with a caller asking Greenstock whether Lady Chetwode is in. The butler answers that her ladyship is not at home, but is sure to see Master Savile, his manner suddenly turning gloomy. Later chapters visit Madame Tussaud's, a studio, and Mrs. Ogilvie's, and meet Lord Chetwode and a soothsayer called Zero. Leverson writes Edwardian comedy with wit and ease.
27749-from-jungle-to-java-the-trivial-im:
Arthur Keyser edited these trivial impressions of a short excursion to Netherlands India, as told by Mr. X, an officer in a small Malay state under British protection. Published by the Roxburghe Press, the book follows its narrator from Singapore to Java.

Chapters cover Batavia, Buitenzorg, baths and volcanoes, a model estate, and a quest for a mother that ends at a wodena's house. Light and observant, the book gives a colonial traveler's view of Dutch Java at the turn of the century, with customs, costumes, and local color. The narrator's jungle home lies in a small Malay state, where British officers relieve local rulers of administration.
2789-the-motor-girls-on-a-tour:
Margaret Penrose wrote this Motor Girls adventure, following the success of the Motor Boys series by Clarence Young. Readers had asked for a similar series for girls, and Penrose, author of the Dorothy Dale books, was chosen to furnish these tales.

The Motor Girls tour by car, with mishaps, mysteries, and friendships along the road. Penrose writes in the brisk series style, with plucky heroines and clean fun. The book delights as an early girls' motoring adventure, from an age when a car tour was still a daring feat. The road gives the girls freedom their mothers never knew.
28043-ships-in-harbour:
David Morton's Ships in Harbour, published in 1921 by G. P. Putnam's Sons, is a book of short lyrics first printed in magazines such as Poetry, Harper's, and The Bookman. Morton writes of wooden ships, old houses, gardens, and autumn days, often in a single clear image. The title poem sets the book's quiet, sea-bound mood.

Other poems touch on Napoleon, battlefields, and the passing of kings, but most stay close to home: tea time, rain, a town street, a summer tour. The verse is plain and musical, with little show. Readers who like brief, thoughtful poems will find the book easy to dip into.
28091-the-double-four:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote The Double Four, first published in September 1911, as a set of linked spy tales around Peter Ruff. Ruff now lives as a quiet country gentleman at Aynesford Manor, after years in a world of intrigue he tried to leave behind. A summons from Madame Sogrange pulls him back into secret work.

Ten chapters follow Ruff through embassies, harbours, and hidden societies, from Havana to London drawing rooms. Each tale stands on its own, yet together they show a man torn between a peaceful home life and the old skills that still bind him. The book suits readers who enjoy early spy fiction with a polite, Edwardian surface.
28173-three-young-pioneers-a-story-of-th:
John Theodore Mueller's Three Young Pioneers tells of the early settlement of America through three children. Orphaned on an Atlantic crossing, a boy and his sister find a protector in Mrs. Bradley, who takes them to her quarters and feeds them. The minister blesses her kindness, and the children join a new community.

Later chapters follow the family to a log house, through war with the Pequot Indians, capture and escape, and a Christmas at a trading post. Agnes, a new brother, and old neighbours fill the tale. Mueller writes for young readers, stressing courage, faith, and neighbourly help on the frontier.
28291-our-home-in-the-silver-west-a-stor:
Gordon Stables wrote Our Home in the Silver West as a boys' story of struggle and adventure in South America. A Highland feud drives the heroes from Scotland to Rio, then to an Argentine estancia, where they build a house, lay out gardens, and face Pampa Indians, earthquakes, and a tiger. The Religious Tract Society published the tale for young readers.

Chapters follow a terrible ride, a journey like a dream, a tragedy at a fonda, and a last assault on the estancia. Stables, a naval surgeon turned author, writes with brisk, hearty humour. The book offers old-style imperial adventure, with danger, loyalty, and a new home in the west.
28752-pleasures-of-the-telescope-an-illu:
Garrett P. Serviss wrote this 1901 guide for people who own a telescope and want to know what to look at. It opens with plain advice on choosing and testing a glass, explaining the difference between reflectors and refractors and how a telescope is made to show true color. Later chapters walk through the sky by season, naming the constellations and the sights within them.

Readers learn where to find Orion and its wonders, the star fields of Virgo, the summer stars of Scorpio and Hercules, and the planets and double stars worth a night's attention. Many pictures help the beginner aim and judge what is seen. The book still works as an entry point to backyard astronomy, written for general readers rather than trained scientists.
2922-the-past-condition-of-organic-natur:
Thomas Henry Huxley delivered this lecture to working men at the Museum of Practical Geology in 1863, as the second of six on Darwin's Origin of Species. Huxley first sketches the present condition of organic nature, summing up the multiplicity of animal forms and the broad principles visible to an attentive eye. He then turns backward, asking what the rocks and fossils say about earlier life.

The lecture warns against easy readings of the strata, noting that one layer may have been laid down ages before another despite appearances. Huxley cites Sir Henry De la Beche on that fallacy and works through figures to make the point. The talk remains a clear example of Victorian science teaching, plain in language and careful in argument.
30476-zero-hour:
Alexander Blade writes a boy's rocket adventure in which Bobby learns by accident that a rocket is about to be shot to the Moon and wants to go along. His father has already left for the project, and at four o'clock the great day arrives, though Bobby must keep the big secret at breakfast.

His mother drinks coffee and studies a fashion catalogue across the table, glad to be occupied, while Bobby stays silent for fear of spilling what he knows. At Buffalo Flats, secrets rule: top scientists do not discuss their work even with their wives, and wives never ask. Blade turns that secrecy into suspense, as Bobby wonders whether he can smuggle himself aboard.
30827-the-count-s-chauffeur:
William Le Queux wrote this 1907 adventure novel, first in Nash's Summer Library of Popular Novels, about a man known across half of Europe as the Count's Chauffeur. Its narrator is George Ewart, an Englishman of cosmopolitan birth, whose father worked as an agent for a London firm on the Continent. At twenty George tried City life, but a high stool, a dusty ledger, and sandwich lunches held no charm for him.

His turn for mechanics points him toward cars and the road. Eleven chapters follow a move on the Forty, a sentimental swindle, a secret, a run with Rosalie, and the peril of Pierrette. Le Queux mixes motoring, romance, and intrigue across Paris, Rome, Florence, Berlin, and Vienna. Readers who enjoy Edwardian thrillers will find a fast, worldly tale told by a driver at the heart of the action.
31416-the-immortal-moment-the-story-of-k:
May Sinclair's novel The Immortal Moment, published by Doubleday, Page and Company in October 1908 and illustrated by C. Coles Phillips, tells the story of Kitty Tailleur. Kitty is a young woman whose face, in an early illustration, pleads with its own reflection in a glass, a hint of the inward drama Sinclair builds around her. The novel follows Kitty through love, choice, and the single moment that gives the book its title.

Sinclair, already known for The Helpmate and The Divine Fire, writes with close attention to a woman's inner life and to the social world that presses on it. Readers of Edwardian fiction will find a compact, psychological novel rather than a plot-driven romance. Its interest lies in how one brief, decisive experience reshapes a life.
31472-cynthia-s-chauffeur:
Louis Tracy's Cynthia's Chauffeur was published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York with illustrations by Howard Chandler Christy. It opens on Derby Day, the first Wednesday in June, when London is gay with its annual holiday. Tracy, author of The Wings of the Morning and A Son of the Immortals, begins with a hired car and a first day's run. He soon introduces Cynthia Vanrenen, who breaks in excitedly upon a conversation about her circumstances. The Great Question of the day, besides the weather, hangs over the city.

The novel that follows is a romance of motors, society, and adventure, with a chauffeur at the center of Cynthia's story. Tracy writes the popular fiction of his day with pace and polish. Readers who enjoy Edwardian romance will find a lively tale, where a car, a holiday crowd, and a young woman's choices drive the plot.
32004-the-knights-of-arthur:
Frederik Pohl's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in January 1958, gives a would-be king a single suitcase for a kingdom. Its tagline says Arthur is in desperate need of armed henchmen, because his keys to a kingdom are typewriter keys. The narrator travels with Arthur, while a third man, Engdahl, crosses by another route. The three split up to avoid drawing attention.

The opening scenes play the joke straight. The narrator registers at a hotel claiming to be from Chicago. He tips a bellboy a hundred and fifty dollars, and warns him that his baggage is booby-trapped. Philadelphia, he notes, is no longer all the fashion, as it was a couple of years before. The story is a comic science-fiction take on kingship, loyalty, and old claims of power in a changed America.
32086-japan-a-record-in-colour:
Mortimer Menpes's Japan, A Record in Colour, transcribed by Dorothy Menpes and published in London by Adam and Charles Black in December 1901, records Japan through an artist's eyes. It was reprinted in May 1902 and again in 1903, 1904, and 1905, and dedicated to Lady Edward Cecil, whose sympathy Menpes credits with much of his work's success in Japan. Colour illustrations face the text throughout, from a frontispiece called Miss Pomegranate onward.

The chapters move through art and the drama, living art, and painters and their methods, to art in practical life, gardens, and flower arrangement. Later chapters cover the geisha, children, workers, and national characteristics, with illustrations of actors, temples, streets, and summer afternoons. Readers get a visual, personal record of Japan at the turn of the century, written by a painter rather than a historian.
32234-the-lion-of-janina-or-the-last-day:
Maurus Jokai's The Lion of Janina, or The Last Days of the Janissaries, translated by R. Nisbet Bain, was published in New York and London by Harper and Brothers in 1898. Its copyright dates from 1897. Jokai, author of The Green Book and Black Diamonds, writes of the late Janissary age. The lion of the title is Ali Tepelenti, the Pasha of Janina, met as a fugitive facing dust and ashes tomorrow.

Its chapters run from The Caverns of Seleucia and Eminah through A Turkish Paradise, Gaskho Bey, and A Man in the Midst of Dangers. They continue to The Lion in the Fox's Skin, The Albanian Family, and The Pen of Mahmoud. Later chapters: The Circassian and His Family, The Avenger, The Flowers of the Garden of Begtash, The Shipwreck of Leonidas, and A Ball in the Seraglio. Readers get a romance, where Janissaries call themselves flowers from Begtash's garden.
32556-dorothy-s-tour:
Evelyn Raymond's Dorothy's Tour, copyrighted in 1912, sends Dorothy from Bellevieu to New York, Washington, and beyond. A letter from New York excites her, and within two weeks she starts for the city, where Mr. Ludlow will meet her and Aunt Betty.

Chapters follow preparations, a Carnegie concert, the opera, a dread call in the night, a locket, and the tour itself, with Washington, Mount Vernon, and a lake city along the way. An accident and a conclusion close a story of travel, music, and the high honors of a young American girl on tour.
34188-with-our-fighting-men-the-story-of:
William E. Sellers wrote this story of fighting men's faith, courage, and endurance in the Great War. It appeared in London by the Religious Tract Society, with coloured and other illustrations from drawings and photographs. Sellers, author of From Aldershot to Pretoria, follows soldiers from home base to front.

Chapters run from early days at the front and the fighting base through the Marne, the Aisne, and Ypres to Thomas Atkins in the trenches. Christmas at the front, Christian heroism, and the sign of the Red Cross follow. Sellers writes of faith under fire with warmth. The book offers a chaplain's view of the war.
35183-memorials-of-the-sea-my-father-bei:
Memorials of the Sea: My Father is a biography of William Scoresby of Whitby, written by his son, the Reverend William Scoresby. It was published in London in 1851 by Longman and its partners. The father was a merchant seaman of Whitby. The son, a clergyman and fellow of the Royal Societies of London and Edinburgh, gathered the records of his adventurous life.

The dedication tells how the book came to be. Lady Matilda Maxwell first saw the father's unusual character from report alone, when he was known to her only by name. Her deep interest, and her repeated requests for the story of his deeds, led the son to collect the records. The result is a son's memorial of a father's life at sea: voyages, dangers, and character, preserved by the one man placed to tell them with both knowledge and love.
36244-latitude-19-a-romance-of-the-west-:
Mrs Schuyler Crowninshield set her romance Latitude 19 in the West Indies in the year 1820. D Appleton and Company issued the novel in New York in 1898, with pictures by George Gibbs. The title page calls the tale a faithful account of the painful adventures of five people.

The Skipper, the Bo's'n, the Smith, the Mate, and Cynthia are cast ashore against their will. Pirates return, a villain dies, a prisoner escapes, and the Bo's'n hides treasure. Later chapters bring a black king, a fight, and a task taken on to win back liberty. Sea peril, capture, and rescue drive the plot across twenty-two chapters.
36487-the-night-riders-a-thrilling-story:
Henry Wood wrote The Night Riders, billed as a thrilling story of love, hate, and adventure depicting the tobacco uprising in Kentucky. A frontispiece shows a woman dressed in her husband's clothes leading men to the tobacco barn. Mottoes warn that a fence between makes love more keen, and that hatred hatched in the bosom breeds snakes.

The novel dramatises the night rider troubles, when masked men enforced the tobacco growers' cause by violence. Love and hate are promised equal room with the raids. Readers get a popular novel of the Kentucky tobacco wars, written close to the events it turns into melodrama.
36624-adventures-of-working-men-from-the:
Adventures of Working Men was written by George Manville Fenn. Cassell and partners published it in London. Its subtitle adds: from the notebook of a working surgeon. Chapter one is called My Patients. The surgeon narrator has had patients enough in a busy life. Of all of them, he says, give him the genuine working man. Sick or hurt, such a man endures with hope and childlike faith. Wealthy patients, by contrast, expect months of illness cured in hours.

His own practice was mixed, and fate took him about the country. He filled in for other doctors on holiday or ill. Take him all in all, he writes, the British workman is sterling. The tales that follow test that rule in case after case.
3694-every-man-in-his-humour:
Ben Jonson, the rival and friend of Shakespeare, wrote this comedy of London life around the old notion of humours, the idea that each person is ruled by one ruling bent. A jealous merchant, a fretful father, and a swaggering soldier cross paths with a crew of young gallants in shops, streets, and homes. Each acts out his fixed folly while others scheme to profit from it. The play mixes sharp talk with slapstick, and its jokes land through character rather than plot twists.

Jonson first staged the piece in 1598, and it helped make his name as a comic writer. The long opening essay in this edition sketches his hard youth, his schooling under William Camden, and his rise among the players. Readers new to Jonson get a lively way into his world, where vanity, greed, and love all wear the same city clothes and trip over each other.
3695-every-man-out-of-his-humour:
Ben Jonson writes a comedy of humours, performed in 1599 as a companion to his earlier Every Man in His Humour. The play's characters are out of their humour, meaning out of balance, and Jonson satirizes courtiers, poets, soldiers, and gallants who mistake fashion for nature. An introduction sketches Jonson himself, a large man who as a youth enlisted as a soldier, trailing his pike in Flanders in the wars of William the Silent against Spain.

Jonson later became a literary dictator and poet laureate, shaping English letters more than any man of his time. His comedy mixes sharp verse with stage business and direct address to the audience. The play suits readers interested in Elizabethan theater and in Jonson's bold, combative art.
37292-thoughts-for-the-quiet-hour:
Moody gathered a book of daily readings that Revell copyrighted in 1900. A note to the reader praises a bright sign of the times. Many Christians in the young people's societies, it says, now keep a quiet hour each day, going apart to be alone with God.

The pieces first ran month by month in a journal of Christian work. They are short thoughts set to light up the verses they hang on. An index of texts at the back runs through the whole Bible. The book is made for the desk and the pocket: one text, one thought, and a still few minutes to take them in.
37387-letters-to-severall-persons-of-hon:
John Donne's Letters to Severall Persons of Honour appear here in the Sturgis and Walton edition of 1910, limited to six hundred copies. Charles Edmund Merrill edited the text with notes. His note explains that Donne's son collected and published the letters in 1651, twenty years after the poet's death, in their original form here reprinted for the first time. Sales were small; the sheets were rebound three years later as a second edition, and few copies of either survive.

Merrill corrected punctuation only where sense required it, and used manuscripts, through Edmund Gosse's kindness, for a few letters. The frontispiece engraving shows Donne at forty, after the portrait prefixed to the Poems of 1633. The edition is dedicated to Payson Merrill, with a Latin tag from Horace. Gosse's Life and Letters of Donne is acknowledged as the study every later student works under.
37958-stones-of-the-temple-or-lessons-fr:
A devotional work takes lessons from the fabric and furniture of the temple, issued by Rivingtons at London and Oxford. The title promises stones that teach. Church architecture books of this kind read altars, fonts, and screens as sermons in material form. Victorian writers found doctrine in every part of a church building. The temple here is both the Jerusalem original and its churchly heirs.

Such books served clergy preparing sermons and laity visiting old churches. They joined archaeology to devotion. The Rivingtons house specialized in church literature. This volume's lessons turn craftsmanship into theology for general readers. Its Greek motto text survives in the transcription's character notes.
37962-plays-lady-frederick-the-explorer-:
Maugham takes the stage in a volume of plays that opens with Lady Frederick, a comedy in three acts, printed in London in 1912. Heinemann made the book, in his Modern Plays run. The Explorer and A Man of Honour stand with it in the volume, by the title.

Lady Frederick was produced at the Court Theatre on Saturday, October 26, 1907, a cast list states. Ethel Irving played Lady Frederick Berolles, and Edmund Breon played Sir Gerald O'Mara. A marchioness and marquess of Mereston, a captain, and an admiral fill the named parts. A dressmaker, a footman, a maid, and a waiter serve the house. Stage readers get the comedy as printed for the Heinemann list, with its first cast kept on record.
38586-mr-punch-s-cockney-humour:
Mr Punch’s Cockney Humour picks the cream of London jokes from Punch magazine. J A Hammerton edited the Punch Library of Humour set. The Educational Book Company issued this volume with one hundred thirty three pictures. Phil May, Charles Keene, and George Du Maurier drew for it.

Punch had run from eighteen hundred forty one when the set was made. Twenty five theme books sort its best jokes by kind. Life in London, at the seaside, and on tour fill kin volumes. Coster lads Bill and his mate trade cracked word play here. Arry at Hampstead Heath rages in verse at a tube line scheme. All’s swell that ends swell, Arry quips of his misfit boots. Dropped aitches and street slang rule each joke and rhyme. The Cockney stands as Punch’s pet butt and pet hero both.
39001-social-transformations-of-the-vict:
Social Transformations of the Victorian Age, published in 1897, is Escott's survey of court and country in late Victorian England. The book follows his England: Its People, Polity and Pursuits, without repeating it. Escott works by observation, helped by experts in each field. Friends who aided him in the seventies, among them Sir Charles Dilke, helped again in the nineties.

He calls the book a survey, not a history: a set of views from one standpoint. Sketches show national life and institutions at work. The earlier volume had been translated into several European languages. It was even adopted as a text book in the higher grade state schools of Germany. This sequel carries the picture down to 1897.
39968-lancashire-humour:
Lancashire Humour, by Thomas Newbigging, was printed in London by J M Dent and Company in 1901, with plates by J Ayton Symington. A first edition came out in December 1900 and a second in April 1901. Newbigging gives the book to his dear wife, a gradely Lancashire lass.

He opens with a line from Songs of the Wilsons, come, Robin, sit down, and I will tell thee a tale. To find the pure Lancashire character, he says, seek the eastern border of the county, where it joins the West Riding of Yorkshire. A line from Manchester by Bolton and Blackburn to Clitheroe cuts the slice. Oldham, Bury, Rochdale, the Rossendale Valley, and the country to Burnley and Colne hold the choicest examples. Dialect fans get tales and talk from the mill towns in their own speech.
40214-the-swan-and-her-crew-or-the-adven:
The Swan and Her Crew is a boys' adventure book by Christopher Davies, telling of three young naturalists and sportsmen on the Broads and rivers of Norfolk. This is the second edition, printed in London by Frederick Warne, with numerous illustrations. A frontispiece shows the boys hawking on the Broad.

Davies opens with a chatty preface. A preface, he says, is like the bow of an actor or the handshake of two friends, the prelude to the entertainment. He hopes the reader will answer that he is quite well, and much the better for the meeting. He offers to answer questions from young readers who want more on the subjects of the book. The Swan is the boys' boat, and the tale joins sailing, sport, and the study of birds and beasts on the Norfolk waters.
40593-school-room-humour:
School Room Humour, by Macnamara, a doctor and member of Parliament, is a joke book drawn from school life. Arrowsmith printed the third edition at Bristol in 1913; the first came in 1905. Macnamara thanks the directors of the Schoolmaster magazine for most of the stories, and his old friends the teachers up and down the country for their anecdotes.

A motto on the title page, from Truthful James, aged ten, defines faith as what makes you believe what you know to be untrue. Chapters sort the material: children's witticisms, a budget of quaint definitions, children's letters, the religious difficulty, the fond parent, and little scientists at sea. One opening scholar gives BC as Before Christ, then tops it by giving BA as Before Adam.
41343-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The Encyclopaedia Britannica eleventh edition fills this volume from Italy to Jacobite Church. A set of fixes at the front shows the care taken with its text. In the article Italy, a line tells how secret societies replied to persecution. The Carbonari and their fellows assassinated brutal officials and spies, it says. Garibaldi beat a surprise attack on Rome, and might have driven the French into the sea.

The article Ivory gives Sir James Ivory, who left the church for teaching. In 1786 he became a teacher of mathematics and natural philosophy at Dundee. Ivory crucifixes were turned out in enormous numbers, the article adds. Helen Maria Jackson, the poet who wrote as Helen Hunt, stands in the volume too. The book gives the great reference work in its classic form, article by learned article.
41762-the-queer-the-quaint-and-the-quizz:
Frank H Stauffer compiled a cabinet for the curious, copyrighted in 1882 in Philadelphia, with a motto from Byron that the company is mixed. A rhymed list promises oddities and wonders, antiquities and blunders, omens, mystic fire, and strange customs. The introduction strings quotes on superstition from many writers. One passage calls superstition an empire stretching across all ages of human history.

Stauffer notes that a shooting star can spoil a night's rest for some. A man in love may grow pale at the plucking of a merry thought, a wishbone. Nothing is so small, he argues, that a mind full of omens cannot make it dreadful. The book gathers lore, freaks, and cranks for browsing.
41939-rosa-bonheur:
Crastre wrote this life of Rosa Bonheur, the animal painter, in French. Cooper Englished it for Stokes in New York in 1913. Eight colour plates show her work, in a Masterpieces in Colour set. Plate one shows a lion meditating, from her own museum piece.

Artists call the lion the hardest of all beasts to paint. Bonheur caught the fugitive face looks of the kingly beast well. A menagerie visit let her record them with vigour and truth. Reynolds, Turner, and Raphael stand among sister volumes in the set. Her dates, 1822 to 1899, stand on the series title page with her name.
42236-jewels-of-gwahlur:
Robert Howard wrote Jewels of Gwahlur, an adventure tale first published in Weird Tales in March 1935. It is one of his stories of Conan, the hill-born fighter whose strength and climbing skill the opening puts to hard use. The tale starts far from any road, above a sea of jungle.

Conan works his way up sheer cliffs that curve away east and west, their stone glinting in the rising sun. He climbs in short red silk breeks, with sandals, sword, and dagger slung on his back. Holds are no more than niches and knobs, and at times he hangs by his fingernails. He climbs fast despite the risk, pausing to scan the jungle below for any sign of human life.
42515-the-book-of-the-ladies-illustrious:
Pierre de Bourdeille, Abbe de Brantome, portrays court ladies in The Book of the Ladies, or Illustrious Dames, privately printed at New York in 1899 for members of the Versailles Historical Society. The edition calls itself an unexpurgated rendition into English, limited to two hundred copies. An introductory essay by C-A Sainte-Beuve stands at the front.

The discourses proceed queen by queen: Anne de Bretagne, Catherine de Medici, Marie Stuart, Elisabeth of France, and Marguerite of Navarre, with Sainte-Beuve's remarks after several. A final discourse gathers many more ladies of the French and Austrian houses. Court gossip here is history.
42990-in-unfamiliar-england-a-record-of-:
In Unfamiliar England is a travel book of 1910 by Thomas D Murphy. Its full title calls it a record of a seven thousand mile tour by motor. The tour sought out the unfrequented nooks and corners of England. It also made trips into Scotland and Ireland. The book holds sixteen plates in colour and photographs in plenty. Murphy had written an earlier motor book on British highways.

Twenty-one chapters trace the road from London nooks to East Anglia and the midlands. The party ran from Coventry to Exeter and through the west country. Wales, the Byron country, and the Yorkshire coast all get their turns. One chapter crosses the Tweed, and two are given to Ireland. The frontispiece shows Sulgrave Manor, the old home of the Washingtons. The aim is the byway, not the highway.
43223-the-world-s-best-poetry-volume-09-:
The ninth volume of The World's Best Poetry, edited under Bliss Carman and published by Morris at Philadelphia in 1904, holds tragedy and humor together. Gummere's essay opens it, The Old Case of Poetry in a New Court. The tragedy side keeps such anchors as Longfellow's Wreck of the Hesperus. The humor side is rich in dialect and platform verse: Harte's Plain Language from Truthful James and The Society upon the Stanislaus, and Hay's Jim Bludso and Little Breeches.

Holmes contributes the One-Horse Shay, and Leland his Hans Breitmann's Party. The copyright notices at the front, usually skipped, here serve as a roll of honor for the anthology's permissions. Charlotte Perkins Gilman's A Conservative stands for the newer wit. Ten volumes sorted the world's poetry by mood, home, love, sorrow, nature, and the higher life among them. Volume Nine was the one that made readers laugh after making them weep.
43576-an-introduction-to-entomology-vol-:
William Kirby and William Spence wrote An Introduction to Entomology, elements of the natural history of insects. This fifth edition was printed in London in 1828, in four volumes of which this is the first. The authors gave the work to Sir Joseph Banks, whose unrivalled library furnished much of its most interesting matter.

Since the first edition, generic names changed greatly as old genera split into natural groups and subgenera, the advertisement explains. New names are generally adopted here, and an improved index may be had separately by owners of former editions. One cause of little attention to entomology in this country opens the preface argument. Insect science readers get a founding text.
43577-an-introduction-to-entomology-vol-:
An Introduction to Entomology, volume two, is the fifth edition, of 1828, of the letters on the natural history of insects by Kirby and Spence. Written as letters to a young friend, the work became the standard English gateway to the study of insects. The volume's letters concern the societies of insects, their defences, motions, noises, light, winter sleep and instinct.

Seven letters follow the social insects: the imperfect societies, then the perfect ones of white ants and ants, wasps and humble-bees, and two long letters on the hive-bee. Letter sixteen opens by congratulating the reader on wanting more than a cabinet of named specimens. The history and economy of insects, the letter urges, are the real prize, in the line of Swammerdam, Ray, Réaumur and the Hubers. The tone is that of a rector naturalist preaching the wonders of creation through its smallest works.
43578-an-introduction-to-entomology-vol-:
William Kirby and William Spence set out the outer build of insects in volume three of their classic survey, dated 1826. Longman and partners in Paternoster Row printed the work in London, with plates. A portrait of Kirby, printed by H Howard and engraved by W T Fry, fronts the volume.

A note at the front grants that the last volumes came late through the ill health of one author. Spence had drafted each letter in his share years before, yet new facts had to be worked in by Kirby alone. Thousands of specimens, many checked more than once, fed the letters on outer anatomy. The authors hope slips that crept in stay small and leave the main claims sound. Tables of terms span pages 354 to 393 of this volume.
43579-an-introduction-to-entomology-vol-:
An Introduction to Entomology, volume four, sets out the inner anatomy and working of insects, by William Kirby and William Spence. The work, in four volumes here in a fifth edition issued at London in 1828, is written as a series of letters. A portrait of Spence, painted and engraved by named artists, fronts this volume. The contents open with the thirty seventh letter.

That letter treats the inner build of insects under the head of sensation. Letters on breathing, on the flow of the blood, and on digestion follow in order. Secretion and reproduction carry the survey through the body's hidden work. Kirby, a clergyman naturalist, and Spence built the first great English account of insect life. Their letters taught a generation to see the insect as a working machine of fine parts.
44426-stories-of-the-days-of-king-arthur:
Stories of the Days of King Arthur is a retelling of the Arthur tales by Charles Henry Hanson, meant for boy readers. Hanson's preface sets out his plan in full. From the great mass of tales that grew round Arthur over the ages, he picks those most fit to catch a young mind. He casts them as a linked tale in due order of events. So far as he can, he keeps the quaint style of Malory. At the same time he keeps the sense clear.

Hanson hopes the book will serve as a first step to the romances themselves. It should help boys read Malory's great prose work with profit. It should also ease their way into the Poet Laureate's poems on Arthur. Some turns of the old tales are unfit for young hands, he notes. Those he leaves out.
44492-whip-and-spur:
George Waring published his horse sketches Whip and Spur with Doubleday, Page in 1904, under an 1897 copyright. Contents name the pieces plainly, Vix, Ruby, and Wettstein among them. Campaigning with Max, How I Got My Overcoat, Two Scouts, and Fox-Hunting in England fill out the table. Most tales turn on one horse and what that horse taught its rider.

Vix opens in the spring of 1858, as work on Central Park fairly commenced. Waring argues himself into needing a saddle horse on a park salary with a family to feed. Auctions, false ads, and broken down brutes fill his hunt for blood at a fair price. Cigars gave way to a pipe to pay the keep. Horsemen get shrewd, funny counsel throughout.
44608-the-ba-bur-na-ma-in-english-memoir:
Annette Susannah Beveridge turned the memoirs of Bābur from their Turki text into English, first printed in 1922. Bābur, full name Z̤ahiru'd-dīn Muḥammad Bābur Pādshāh Ghāzī, wrote his own life tale. A note warns that names in Turki, Arabic, and Persian take many forms in the text.

The first part treats Farghāna, from the year 899 of the Hijra, when Bābur took his father's seat as a boy. His father's death, his uncles' attacks, and his first moves on Samarkand fill year by year notes. Beveridge opens with a long preface on Bābur's models in peace, the torn state of the tale, and old copies of the work.
44704-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Volume twenty of The World’s Greatest Books is given to miscellaneous literature, and it carries the index of the set. Arthur Mee and Hammerton were the joint editors of the whole work. A portrait of Matthew Arnold fronts this closing volume. Addison and the Spectator open the contents at page one.

Aesop and his fables stand next in the list of selections. Arnold’s Essays in Criticism and the Main Currents of Brandes follow. Burton’s Anatomy of Melancholy and Carlyle on heroes fill the middle pages. A complete index of all twenty volumes stands at the end of the book. Such sets promised a whole library in condensed, guided form. This last volume sweeps the odd corners of letters into the plan.
46168-experiments-and-observations-tendi:
William Watson reports his electrical experiments in letters to Martin Folkes and to the Royal Society. Davis, printer to the Society, published the collection in London in 1746 at one shilling. The papers were meant for the Philosophical Transactions, in the order they were read.

Watson's preface tells how a small private printing, made for impatient friends, raised a public demand beyond expectation. He broke up that press, then sent the sheets to press a second time before officious gentlemen did it for him. The experiments repeat before witnesses of rank, with Folkes advising throughout. Sloane, as Copley's executor, appointed Watson to receive the Society's annual gold prize medal.
46381-the-lead-of-honour:
The Lead of Honour, a novel by Norval Richardson, came out in 1910. Four printings in four months show the speed of its first sale. A colour front plate by Frank Merrill heads the Grosset edition. The tale is built in three books with set names for each. The Schoolmaster, the Lawyer, and the Lover mark its three parts.

Chapter heads trace a life from youth and high aims onward. Juleps and politics and a house of Spaniards fill the school part. The law part holds a first case and a hanging threat. Seven years pass before the lover's part of the tale starts. Slaves staked at cards and a wedding near prison bars appear. Sargent Everett, shown in the front plate, ends as the honourable man.
47548-human-bullets-a-soldier-s-story-of:
Human Bullets is a soldier story of Port Arthur by Tadayoshi Sakurai, a lieutenant in the Japanese army. Count Okuma wrote the opening. Masujiro Honda turned it into English and Alice Mabel Bacon shaped it, and Houghton Mifflin printed it in 1907.

Chapters run from call up and departure through a dangerous landing to the value of Port Arthur. The battle of Nanshan and its aftermath stand early. Later parts treat digging and scouting, first captives, and a fight at Waitu Shan. Camp life and brave men and their memorials fill the mid part. Sakurai writes as a man who fought in the siege in the war with Russia. Readers get war at ground level from the Japanese side.
48169-the-post-of-honour:
Richard Wilson told The Post of Honour, stories of daring deeds done by men of the British Empire in the Great War. J M Dent and Sons published it at London and Toronto in 1917. Nurse Cavell with her dogs fronts the book. A chapter on the Victoria Cross opens the contents. Captain Grenfell and the charge of the Lancers come first. British sailors who knew how to die follow.

Some of the first V C's and the spirit of Sir Philip Sidney stand early. Corporal Holmes, the men of the first line, and the Canadian Scottish come next. Anzac and submarines in the Dardanelles fill the middle. The story of Edith Cavell and Jack Cornwell, the boy who carried on, stand at the heart. Heroes of Loos and the Canadians at Vimy Ridge close toward the end.
48573-british-and-foreign-arms-armour:
Charles Henry Ashdown surveys the fighter's kit in British and Foreign Arms and Armour, from T C and E C Jack of London in 1909. The book carries 450 engravings in the text and 42 plates. They are drawn from actual examples, brasses, and effigies, and from research in the British Museum, the Tower of London, and the Wallace Collection.

The contents march by period: weapons of prehistoric man, the Assyrians, the Romans, Saxons and Danes, and the Norman age. Then the chain mail centuries unfold in their named styles, cyclas, studded and splinted, camail and jupon, down to Maximilian armour and the half-armour after 1600.
49030-the-motor-boat-club-at-the-golden-:
H Irving Hancock takes his motor boat boys to San Francisco Bay in a 1909 series tale. The Henry Altemus Company issued it at Philadelphia. Tom Halstead leads the club, with Joe Dawson at the engine.

The contents promise fog, chase, and capture. Tom is let into a secret early. A hunt runs through the under-world of the docks. A call sounds out of the fog. A fire drill turns earnest. Cragthorpe proves more than troublesome, then shows his real self. A find waits in the forehold. At last a stern looms up in the fog for the chase of their lives. Hancock wrote shelf loads of boys' series books. His heroes are clean, brave, and quick with a wrench or a wheel.
49098-larkspur:
Jane Abbott wrote this girls' novel, copyrighted in 1919 by Lippincott and reissued by Grosset and Dunlap. Abbott had earlier written 'Happy House' and 'Keineth' for young readers. She dedicates the story to the flowers of her own garden, a note that matches the flower name of the title.

An October day opens the contents, and a captain's story follows in chapter two. Renée finds a home, gardens bloom, and first aid and scouts enter the tale in turn. Aunt Pen plans, breadwinners work and a new lodger arrives, before a Christmas party, a letter from France and a lost baby carry the war-era story on.
49309-mr-punch-s-scottish-humour:
Mr Punch's Scottish Humour is an anthology of jokes, anecdotes and cartoons about Scotland drawn from the magazine Punch, issued in the Punch Library of Humour under editor Hammerton. The volume carries 132 illustrations by Punch artists including Charles Keene, George du Maurier, Phil May and Harry Furniss. The series aimed to gather the best of the magazine's comedy, from its founding in 1841 onward, into themed volumes.

The introduction opens with a story from the Inverness post office, where a clerk objects to letters addressed Inverness, N B, as if London would tolerate S B. The editors answer the old charge that Scots lack humour with their own figures. The Scots, the book argues, laugh at themselves as readily as anyone, and the collection that follows is offered as the proof.
49563-the-lost-land-of-king-arthur:
Cuming Walters wrote The Lost Land of King Arthur, published in London by Chapman and Hall in 1909 with 16 pictures. A photograph of King Arthur's Castle and Execution Rock at Tintagel faces the title page. Two quotes frame the quest: Professor Rhys on the great figure behind the man, and Bacon on the truth that made Arthur famous.

Ten chapters tour the lands tied to the legend. They cover the king and his old chroniclers, the lost land of Lyonnesse, Merlin, Tintagel, and Caerleon-upon-Usk. Later chapters take up the Round Table and Arthur's battles, Camelot, the Holy Grail, and the last battle near Camelford. The book closes at Glastonbury with the passing of Arthur. Readers who love the legend get a walk through its real places.
49713-fifteen-hundred-miles-an-hour:
Charles Dixon edits a tale of a flight to Mars issued at London in 1895. Bliss, Sands and Foster published it at Craven Street. Captain Arthur Layard, late of the Royal Engineers, drew the pictures.

Chapter one states the inventor's claim. A lifetime of experiments backs him, he tells Temple. Every design stands worked out to its simplest detail in his book. Only capital is wanting. The ship Sirius then leaves Earth in chapter two. Beyond the clouds come awful moments and the glories of the heavens. Mars brings a strange world, captivity, and a death sentence. The desert Chados, the crag Remagaloth, and the temple on the hill Verosi mark the road. Love and jealousy drive the close, ending in a wedding.
51244-the-livestock-producer-and-armour:
The Livestock Producer and Armour is a booklet put out by Armour and Company of Chicago in 1920. A quote from Philip D Armour heads it, that the success of capital lies in serving the people, not in taking advantage of them. Portraits of the directors stand near the front.

The first part asks how and why the livestock market grew. In the good old days, it says, the local butcher shop set the whole demand for fat stock. A stockman might drive his cattle to the village and find a neighbor had glutted the market with two or three beasts. No price at all could be had that day. Great packing houses, the book argues, made the market nation wide. Farm and trade readers get the packer case in plain terms.
51341-nine-thousand-miles-on-a-pullman-t:
Shaw's account follows a tour of railroad conductors from Philadelphia to the Pacific Coast and back, 9,000 miles on a Pullman train. Allen, Lane and Scott printed the book at Philadelphia in 1898.

Shaw dedicates it to the wives of the party, the beloved companions of their hearths and homes. The picture index alone maps the journey: Broad Street Station, a wreck by train robbers on the Southern Pacific, the Mount Lowe railway, San Francisco, and the Columbia River. Portraits of committee men and conductors fill out the record. Shaw signs himself yours truly on the frontispiece. The party crossed the Columbia River on the ferry Tacoma.
51468-the-love-of-monsieur:
George Gibbs wrote The Love of Monsieur, held in 1903 at New York. Gibbs had writ The Yellow Dove and The Bolted Door. Sixteen chapters carry the tale. The first scene sits in the Fleece Tavern. Talk there turns at once to a French man named Mornay.

Men at the tavern call Mornay a blade of the French Embassy. They say he has luck at chance and with women of all ranks. Mistress Barbara dances in the next chapter and draws his eye. Flight, a ship named the Saucy Sally, a foe in the house, and capture fill the middle. Mutiny and a maroon close the late plot. The tale mixes love with sea risk.
52217-young-hunters-in-porto-rico-or-the:
Captain Ralph Bonehill wrote this boys tale of a hunt for lost treasure. The book came out in Chicago in 1900 with Donohue. It follows the Gun and Sled Club from a past winter tale. One member now owns a yacht, and a sea trip follows.

On Porto Rico the boys hear of Spanish gold hid in caves near Caguas. A hunt starts at once, with stirring adventures on land and sea. Bonehill says he also shows the island as travelers then saw it. He praises its mild air and beauty for future tourists from the States.
52854-knights-in-armour:
Edward Woods, chaplain of the Royal Military College at Sandhurst, wrote this 1916 book to give young officers a Christian picture of their calling. The Chief of the Imperial General Staff, Robertson, commends it in a foreword dated 14 August 1916. In war there are no sham fights, and leaders feel the need of more than knowledge of their profession. Sound religious conviction, he holds, is part of every soldier's equipment.

Woods opens with Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table, whose vows Tennyson made famous in the Idylls of the King. Soldiers, he argues, inherit that knightly ideal, and the greatest soldiers have often been knights of the Cross. The chapters take up four virtues in turn: courage, chivalry, purity, and loyalty. The book is dedicated to the officers and cadets of Sandhurst who made their padre's task easier.
53094-outline-of-the-history-of-the-engl:
The Outline of the History of the English Language and Literature was published by Chambers of London and Edinburgh in 1882. The preface states its object in its title, and then asks for more. The book aims not merely to state facts, but to excite an interest in English philology and in the leading authors who have used the English tongue since Caedmon.

The contents open with the vocabulary of English. First comes the family of the language: the Teutons, High German and Low German, and the Scandinavian tongues. Then the periods divide the story, Anglo-Saxon, Early English, Middle English, and Modern English. The foreign elements follow: the Keltic element, the Latin element in its two periods, and the Scandinavian element. The preface names the audience: secondary schools, pupil teachers, and private students. Schoolrooms of 1882 got the whole life of English in one small outline.
53697-the-house-of-armour:
Marshall Saunders wrote a long novel dated 1897 that opens in Nova Scotia, the green shore land first called New Scotland. A view of Halifax and its harbor sets the scene. Chapter heads point to homecomings, a lost mother, a stolen pocket book, and love found and lost.

The story ranges over town and shore life, with talks in homes and offices and trips on market day. Names in the chapter list, from Zeb to Judy, hint at a wide cast of kin and neighbors. Grief, faith, and hope sit near the end, with one part named for deep despair and one for a sea crossing.
54462-animal-behaviour:
C Lloyd Morgan wrote Animal Behaviour, shown here in a 1920 London second edition. Morgan had writ The Springs of Conduct and Habit and Instinct. The book holds six long chapters with pictures. Each chapter splits into short parts that build step by step.

Early parts treat cells, plants, and reflex acts. Later parts treat mind, instinct, and smart acts in bugs, birds, and beasts. Social life gets a full chapter on calls, bees, ants, and habit passed on. Feelings, play, and sex close the set. Morgan asks at each step how acts grow and change. The book suits readers who want a clear map of the field.
54664-mother-goose-s-bicycle-tour:
Bonnell wrote and adapted Mother Goose's Bicycle Tour, a book of verses for children, and the title page credits the rhymes to Mary Susan Goose herself. William Briggs of Toronto published it, with the work entered in Canada in 1900. An acrostic poem spells out Alexandra, and a copy was accepted by Queen Alexandra in 1901.

The rhymer sings her ancestress's renown and asks kind indulgence for loose verse and meagre wit. Mother Goose, in this modern dress, takes to the bicycle and tours in rhyme. The book belongs to the years when the safety bicycle filled the roads and even nursery figures had to ride. Young readers get the old Goose on wheels, with verses pitched to make them laugh.
54914-his-glorious-appearing-an-expositi:
His Glorious Appearing, by James Springer White, was printed in 1895. The Review and Herald Publishing Company issued it at Battle Creek, Michigan. This is the eleventh edition, revised and illustrated. Its subtitle names the task: an exposition of Matthew twenty four. Two texts head the title page. The disciples ask for the sign of Christ's coming and the end of the world. Jesus answers that when all these things are seen, it is near, even at the doors.

Signs of the coming fill the middle: falling stars, shaken powers of heaven, and the sign of the Son of Man. The parable of the fig-tree and Noah's time follow. The introduction argues from Amos that God reveals his plans to his prophets. Noah preached warning for one hundred and twenty years.
55625-webster-tourneur:
Plays by Webster and Tourneur gathers four dark plays of old London. John Addington Symonds shaped the book with notes and a front talk. Vizetelly and Company issued it in London in eighteen hundred eighty eight. The Mermaid Series stamp marks this unexpurgated form of the plays.

The White Devil and The Duchess of Malfi speak for Webster’s art. The Atheist’s Tragedy stands in Tourneur’s name in this old set. The Revenger’s Tragedy is now held to be Middleton’s work, a note owns. A long first part tells of the Globe Theatre on Bankside. Straw thatch roofed the stage where Shakespeare’s men played by day. A flag of Saint George flew from its roof at play hours there. Fire from a stage gun burned the house in sixteen hundred thirteen. Tenements rose where the pulled down Globe had stood, by sixteen hundred forty four.
55772-the-peddler-spy-or-dutchmen-and-ya:
The Peddler Spy is a dime novel in the Beadle line of cheap tales. The house in New York sold the semi monthly tales for ten cents each. This tale is number one hundred and seven in the novel line. Its rights line dates the work to the year eighteen sixty six.

The front pages pitch the next sea tale in the line with warm praise. Dutchmen and Yankees clash in the tale of the capture named in its title. Ads in dime books served as the shop front for the whole line of tales. Swift plots and broad types mark the house style of the set. The tale fed rail and camp readers who craved war and chase fare.
55899-kew-gardens-with-24-full-page-illu:
Kew Gardens, printed in London in 1908, pairs painting and text. Mower Martin painted the views, and Hope Moncrieff wrote the account that goes with them. Twenty-four full-page pictures in colour fill the book. The Rhododendron Dell fronts the volume. Contents fall in five chapters: royal residences, Kew in favour, the story of the gardens, the village in and about it, and visiting the gardens.

The plates name the wild garden in spring and the lake. Looking up the Thames, the Pagoda, and the water-lily pond follow. The palace, the Italian garden, the ruined arch, and the azaleas stand among the plates. The palm house, the greenhouse, and the herbaceous ground close the list. The first chapter opens on the Pagoda, seen from many points towering over the well-wooded flat by a winding reach of the Thames. It lends a hint of China to the scene.
56038-port-arthur:
Richard Barry wrote Port Arthur, a monster heroism, published by Moffat, Yard and Company at New York in 1905. Illustrations come from the author's own photographs. Parts ran first in the Century, Everybody's, and Collier's. An introductory chapter sums the investment, siege, and capture of Port Arthur. The city of silence and the invisible army follow.

The Japanese Kitchener fills an early chapter. Camp, 203-Meter Hill, and a son of the soil come next. The bloody angle and a battle in the storm raise the middle. The cremation of a general and courting death under the forts follow. Japan's grand old man and the cost of taking Port Arthur close the book. Barry photographed the great siege as he wrote it.
56076-travels-in-southern-europe-and-the:
