Travels in Southern Europe and the Levant is the journal of Cockerell, kept from 1810 to 1817. His son edited it, and Longmans issued it in 1903. Cockerell was an architect and a fellow of the Royal Academy. He sailed from Plymouth on a despatch vessel. A French prize was taken on the way out. Cadiz, Malta, and the Dardanelles line the first chapter. Constantinople fills the chapters that follow.

Sketching there was dangerous work, he notes. Troy, Delos, and Athens come next on his road. At Aegina he found the famed marbles. Their transport and sale fill whole chapters. Olympia and Bassae yield carved stones as well. Crete and Egypt close the long tour. The journal is a classic of Greek travel.
56215-the-school-four:
The School Four is a school story by Albertus Dudley, published at Boston in 1909. Copeland illustrated it for Lothrop, Lee and Shepard. It belongs to Dudley's Stories of the Triangular League. Dudley also wrote the Phillips Exeter series of sports novels. The first chapter is titled John Smith, President. The idea of the league came from a nimble witted graduate of the Newbury Latin school.

That graduate's common name, John Smith, hid his identity well. Chapters follow the cup, a boy named Archibald Dunn, and recruits for the football squad. The story of Jason and the choosing of a successor fill the middle. A slighted offer and the Newbury game build the contest. Scouts bring news before a fruitless interview. The frontispiece shows a Westcott man clutching the ball over a rival's head.
56557-the-life-and-times-of-alfred-the-g:
Charles Plummer wrote The Life and Times of Alfred the Great, being the Ford Lectures for nineteen one. Oxford's Clarendon Press published the book in nineteen two. Plummer was a fellow and chaplain of Corpus Christi College, Oxford. He dedicated the lectures to the Rev John Earle, Rawlinsonian Professor of Anglo Saxon, his friend and former teacher.

Six lectures fill the volume. Two opening lectures treat the sources for Alfred's life. The third covers his life before he took the throne. The fourth joins his campaigns against the Danes with his civil rule. The fifth and sixth treat his civil rule, schooling, and literary works. A summary and conclusion close the lectures. An appendix adds a sermon on the death of Queen Victoria. History readers get an Oxford scholar's full account of Alfred, his wars, and his books.
56872-minerva-s-manoeuvres-the-cheerful-:
Charles Battell Loomis, author of 'Cheerful Americans,' wrote this comic book, published by Barnes in New York in 1905. Gruger drew the plates, one showing a balloon, a craft named Minerva, a shriek and a shout. The subtitle calls the tale the cheerful facts of a return to nature.

Loomis opens with a preface joke about a hit play and its author called before the curtain. Outdoor life, country air and the mishaps of town folk out of their element supply the fun. The tone stays light, with each chapter a fresh scrape in the open.
59715-the-south-american-tour:
Annie S Peck guides travelers in The South American Tour, issued by Hodder and Stoughton of London in 1914, copyrighted in 1913, and illustrated chiefly from her own photographs. A plate shows the north peak of Mount Huascaran, which Peck climbed on September 2, 1908, higher than Mount McKinley. Peck had written A Search for the Apex of America.

Her dedication hopes the book, by urging travel and acquaintance, will promote trade between the Americas and bind the republics in friendship. She thanks the governments of Bolivia, Chile, and Argentina for aid, without which the work would have been impossible.
59886-adrienne-lecouvreur:
Adrienne Lecouvreur, a play by Scribe and Legouvé, appears here in the Oxford French Series edited by American scholars, published at New York in 1917. Theodore Ely Hamilton of Ohio State University edited the text with an introduction and notes. A portrait of the actress fronts the volume.

The introduction begins with Scribe's life: born at Paris in 1791, trained in law, drawn early to the drama. His first public success came in 1816, and plays then poured from him for two or three theatres at once. Readers get a classic French drama of the stage itself, set out for American students with the help they need in notes.
59972-the-truth-about-port-arthur:
Nojine, a Russian war writer who stood through the siege, told the tale of Port Arthur in a book printed at London in 1908. Captain Lindsay cut and turned it into English. Major Swinton shaped the book. A portrait of General Smirnoff stands at the front.

Three printings came in its first year, April, May and September. A table of names opens the work. Each fort bears two names, the Russian and the local. Pai-yin-shan, Chi-kuan-shan and Erh-lung-shan stand in the list. The writer had stood accredited at the front while the Japanese closed in. His aim, as the title claims, is the plain truth of how the great port fell, against the tales told at home.
60290-the-nineteenth-and-their-times-bei:
Colonel John Biddulph wrote the tale of four horse regiments that bore the number nineteen, printed at London in 1899. The book is given by leave to the Princess of Wales. A quote from the institutes of Timour heads it. The warrior's rights, Timour ordains, shall not be infringed.

Old soldiers, grown grey in service, must keep place and pay, the quote runs. Part one treats the nineteenth light dragoons, Drogheda's Horse, from 1759 to 1763. Contents open with the state of Europe in 1756 and the cry of war with France. The growth of the army and fears of a French landing set the scene for the corps' first years.
60405-the-story-of-the-grail-and-the-pas:
Howard Pyle wrote and drew this fourth and last book of his Arthur tales, printed by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York in 1910. It follows his King Arthur, his Champions of the Round Table, and his Sir Launcelot. A plate of Sir Galahad of the Grail stands near the front.

The foreword maps the road: first Sir Geraint, then the winning of the Holy Grail by Sir Galahad, son of Sir Launcelot. Last comes the passing of Arthur, who beats his foes in royal battle and is slain by one he had wounded to death. Pyle grants that much here is sad, yet holds that not all endings are sad in the same way. His reward, he says, is the reader's seal on the work.
60767-the-armourer-and-his-craft-from-th:
The Armourer and His Craft traces the making of armour from the eleventh century to the sixteenth. A picture at the front shows Venus at the forge of Vulcan, painted about 1600. Money in the text is given in the old shillings and pence of its records, a transcriber explains at the start. Fractions, signs for sums, and marks over letters are all spelled out for the plain text reader.

Five centuries of the craft pass in review, from the mail of the Norman age to the fine plate of the late Gothic and early modern courts. Guild rules, prices, and workshop ways can be traced in such a span. The armourer stands here not as a lone artist but as a tradesman in a trade. Records quoted in the appendices ground the story in bills and orders of the time.
60956-the-life-of-pasteur:
René Vallery-Radot wrote the life of his father-in-law, Louis Pasteur, and Doubleday issued the English translation in 1920. Devonshire translated it from the French. Sir William Osler, regius professor of medicine at Oxford, supplies the introduction. Roux, Pasteur's disciple, supplies the motto: the work is admirable, but one must have lived in his intimacy to know the goodness of his heart.

The first chapter roots the genius in a tannery. Jean Joseph Pasteur, a conscript of 1811 and sergeant-major, became a knight of the Legion of Honour and married into Dôle. Louis was born there in 1822, studied at Arbois, and departed for Paris. Vallery-Radot writes the official life from inside the family and the laboratory. It fixed Pasteur in the world's mind: the chemist who became biology's revolutionary, and the saint of the laboratory bench.
60991-the-connoisseur:
Frank Banta's short science fiction story The Connoisseur ran in Worlds of If in May 1961. Its narrator is a crewman on a crippled starship, where men buy young wives by barter. He tells how he traded for twelve-year-old Lisa. His price was a control knob sawn from the ship's own board, plus a folded painting of the dead Navigator's visions. The tale is told in a flat, boastful voice that never questions the custom it describes.

The humor is dark: the crew keeps stripping the ship that keeps them alive, proud of each small theft, while the dying Navigator's warning about knuckle-heads goes unheeded. Banta lets the narrator convict himself out of his own mouth. The story is a sharp little satire on pride, trade, and slow self-destruction, dressed as a cheerful memoir of shipboard life.
61255-lectures-on-the-rise-and-developme:
Gilbert Scott delivered these lectures on the rise and development of medieval architecture at the Royal Academy, published in London in 1879 in two volumes, this being the first. His preface explains that only half were delivered by him as professor of architecture.

The first seven lectures were given while Professor Cockerell held the chair and Scott, then an associate, helped relieve him in his ill health. Later lectures came after Scott succeeded to the professorship. He warns the set is somewhat disconnected and may repeat facts. Readers get the Gothic Revival's leading architect teaching the history of the style he spent his career restoring and building in.
61269-the-sea-road-to-the-east-gibraltar:
A J Sargent prepared The Sea Road to the East for the Visual Instruction Committee of the Colonial Office. George Philip and Son published it in London in 1912. Six lectures trace the sea route from Gibraltar to Wei-hai-wei, and each lecture had its own set of lantern slides, sold apart from the book.

The committee behind the lectures was chaired by the Earl of Meath and stacked with colonial officials, educators, and the director of the National Gallery. In all, 369 slides went with the set, some of them printed in the book as illustrations, with captions carried over into this text.
61646-lectures-on-the-rise-and-developme:
Gilbert Scott gave talks at the Royal Academy on the rise of church building in the middle ages. Murray of London printed the second volume in 1879. Talk ten goes back to the first churches of Britain. Scott treats the work of the Saxons, the churches raised after the coming of Augustine, and the great minsters of Canterbury and York.

Hexham, Ripon, Brixworth, and the tower of Earls Barton give him his proof stones. Talk eleven takes up the Normans, their church at Caen, and the abbey the Confessor built at Westminster before the Conquest. Talk twelve walks through the great Norman churches, from the Tower chapel to Durham and Tewkesbury. The last talk draws the rules of the craft. Scott sets the arched style against the older beamed one, and shows how doors, windows, and vaults grow from first laws of building.
6172-god-and-my-neighbour:
Robert Blatchford, calling himself Nunquam, dedicates God and My Neighbour to his son Robert Corri Blatchford. His preface takes up the word infidel in capitals, a new name bestowed by Christian gentlemen as reproach, though to his ears it sounds quaint and not unpleasing.

The notorious infidel editor of the Clarion, one true believer calls him, and the words return to Blatchford on a walk along the pleasant Strand with his favorite black pipe. He asks which is worse, demagogue or infidel, and answers he is both. Blatchford writes freethought with humor, pipe smoke, and plain challenge.
61880-the-construction-of-the-small-hous:
Vandervoort Walsh, who taught building at Columbia, wrote a guide to putting up small American homes, printed at New York in 1923 with his own drawings. The first chapter treats the money troubles of the day. High rents after the war had made the want of houses plain.

Contents move through types and costs, and the marks of good stuff to build with. Wood frame work, stone and wood homes, and guards against fire follow. Bad methods of sly builders get a chapter of warnings. Plumbing, heating, lights, trim and roofs each take their turn. Last come the look of the house, its setting, and how to pay for the work.
61910-a-funeral-sermon-preach-d-on-the-d:
William Wigan, chaplain in ordinary to His Majesty and vicar of Kensington, preached a funeral sermon on the death of Lady Elizabeth Cutts. She was wife of Lord Cutts. The sermon was preached at Kensington Church on December fifth, sixteen ninety seven. Walter Kettilby in London printed the pamphlet that same year. The text is from the Book of Numbers, chapter twenty three, verse ten.

The text reads, Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my latter end be like his. Wigan notes that the day fell in Advent, when the church bids folk recall the second coming and judgment. The flock was also to take the Holy Sacrament that day. He ties those themes to grief for a virtuous, devout lady. Readers get a clear case of late Stuart funeral preaching at its most grave and plain.
62253-star-of-panadur:
Albert de Pina and Henry Hasse maroon two spacemen on Europa in Star of Panadur, printed in Planet Stories in March 1943. Jim Brannigan hauls a small silver-furred creature from a cavern, sure it means food for the starving pair. Hugh Betancourt takes the animal gently: three feet tall, six-fingered, with large luminous eyes like beryls and no fear in them.

Flashback fills in the wreck, the gravity-screen torn away as Jupiter caught their ship, and the vanished food supply. Even fed, the men are sunk unless they find oxide crystal to alloy in the portable smelter and mend the prow.
62371-pemrose-lorry-radio-amateur:
Isabel Hornibrook wrote Pemrose Lorry, Radio Amateur, a girls' novel issued in Boston in 1923 by Little, Brown, and Company. The heroine is Una Grosvenor, called Jack by her friends and Uteyan at the Camp Fire. The book opens at dawn in Lenox, where Una greets the sunrise and teases the late spring blooms in her garden.

Twenty five parts mix camp life, horses, songs, and the new thrill of home radio sets. Una rigs an aerial to a pine tree and listens for calls on the air. Friends, fathers, a hidden valley, and a race keep the plot moving. Radio terms are woven into a bright outdoor tale.
63561-wrecked-on-spider-island-or-how-ne:
James Otis wrote a boys' tale of a wreck and a found treasure. A L Burt held the rights in New York in 1896. Twenty-two chapters run from Ned Rogers in Portland to success at the close. A plate shows the wreck of the steam yacht Zoe.

Ned Rogers, homeless and patched, earns food on the wharves of Portland, Maine. Folk think him a runaway, but he has no home to run from, Otis writes. Marooning, ghastly visitors, and treasure hunts crowd his wild road. Boys gain a brisk tale of pluck, sea peril, and luck at last.
63719-the-louvre-fifty-plates-in-colour:
The Louvre: Fifty Plates in Colour is an art book by Konody and Brockwell, printed at New York. The two men also made The National Gallery: One Hundred Plates in Colour. Hare edited this volume. Its fourth plate shows Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa, and the note under it describes her in detail.

Lisa, third wife of Francesco del Giocondo, sits turned three-quarters to her right. Her dark almond eyes look out, and her mouth smiles. A mountainous landscape fills the background. The contents run from the early schools through the Florentine school and the Giottesques. Fra Angelico, Uccello, and Botticelli take their plates. The book is a gallery visit in print.
64264-zero-hour:
Ray Bradbury wrote Zero Hour, printed in Planet Stories for fall nineteen forty seven. The magazine proudly calls it one of the best science fiction stories it has ever seen. Children play a new game across green lawns. Mink, aged seven, is the leader at home. Her mother is Mrs Morris. Rockets flew overhead, but the children played on.

Mink ran into the house, all dirt and sweat, loud and strong for her seven years. She rattled pans and tools into a large sack. The most exciting game ever, she gasped, pink faced. Her mother warned her not to dent the things. What is the name of the game, she called. Invasion, said Mink, and the door slammed. In every yard children brought out knives, forks, and pokers. Bradbury fans get a famed tale of play turning real.
64467-the-manhattaners-a-story-of-the-ho:
The Manhattaners, a story of the hour by Edward S Van Zile, is a novel of New York life published in 1895. Van Zile had written A Magnetic Man and Last of the Van Slacks.

The first chapter opens half an hour after midnight in City Hall Park. Two men stand before the statue of Nathan Hale, the young spy hanged by the British. The older man, careworn and carelessly dressed, warns the handsome youth of twenty-three beside him. Fame, he argues, is largely chance. Other heroes of the Revolution were as self-sacrificing as Hale, yet a republic grateful only in spots has forgotten them. He dubs his friend Richard the Lionheart for the talk. The scene sets the novel's tone of city talk, ambition, and worldly wisdom.
6582-in-the-court-of-king-arthur:
Samuel Lowe writes a boys' Arthur tale around a lad named Allan, who finds a champion, goes forth, and meets the knights of the Round Table. Combats, a tournament, Merlin's message, and the prowess of Tristram fill the early chapters, while later ones send Allan toward King Mark's foul plan and a rescue. A kitchen boy, a stranger, and Sir Launcelot all cross his path.

The tale moves from Camelot to Normandy and back, with Gareth, Galahad, and a beggar tied to the Grail quest. Lowe keeps the story clear and the deeds bold, so young readers can follow the code of knighthood. In the Court of King Arthur is a plain, stirring retelling of old legend for a new young audience.
66076-peace-with-honour:
Sydney C Grier wrote Peace With Honour, issued in Boston in June 1902 with pictures by Alfred Pearse. The book is fifth in the Modern East series, and Grier also wrote In Furthest Ind. The tale opens with Mabel North urging her brother Dick to dress smartly and come out that afternoon. She robs him of his cigar and stands on his newspaper.

Mabel wants Dick to see the serious side of her life before he returns to Kubbet-ul-Haj. Dick jokes that she never gave him a moment's peace while he was home. Contents promise fellow-travellers, a crossing of the frontier, and a man who disappeared. Later chapters bring strained relations, an ultimatum, and a cessation of hostilities.
66473-arthur:
Eugène Sue wrote Arthur, here in an illustrated de luxe edition printed in New York with an 1899 copyright. The contents fall into named groups of chapters. The Curé's Tale leads into the story of Hélène, with a bereavement, an avowal, a letter, a portrait, a pavilion, and a contract. A front set of pictures shows scenes of riding, a fall, and a shot fired at close range.

The Marquise de Penafiel heads the next group, with the opera, a green album, and talk on what the world said. Lord Falmouth heads the last, with plans, a yacht, a voyage, and a combat. The tale itself opens as a found journal. A man hunting a country house in the south of France is sent by his notary to a village curé.
66540-cosmic-saboteur:
Frank Robinson wrote the science fiction story Cosmic Saboteur, first printed in the magazine Imagination in February 1955. The opening blurb lays out the scheme: a young man is beaten until he nearly dies, and the beating is meant to teach him to hate Earth. The hate is not real feeling but training, part of his making as a saboteur.

The story opens in Chicago, where Stan, a boy of 17, gets off the elevated train to walk on a fine spring morning. His brother Larry has urged him to quit his job for a better one at a news service. In a deserted alley by a restaurant, three grown men jump him without a word and set to work on him with care, cutting his face and driving fists into his body. Readers start inside the cruelty that the blurb promised, with its purpose still hidden.
67037-on-the-inaccuracies-which-probably:
Thomas A Welton wrote On the Inaccuracies Which Probably Exist in the Census Returns of Ages, printed at Liverpool in 1876 by T Brakell. Welton was a Fellow of the Statistical Society. Years past he had sought death rates for women at set ages in parts of England for the years 1851 to 1870. That work led to this paper.

Welton found it unsafe to think growth at each age matched growth in the whole. Rates of growth by age jumped in wild ways in one place, he says. Table One shows growth rates to age eighty for men and women. Moves abroad explain part of the jumps, he notes. The paper warns census men and health men to treat age returns with care. False ages skew death rates and plans built on them.
67114-massage-exercises-combined-a-perma:
Massage and Exercises Combined is Albrecht Jensen's permanent physical culture course for men, women, and children, published in New York in 1920 with eighty-six illustrations and deep breathing exercises. Jensen had formerly been in charge of medical massage clinics at Polyclinic Hospital and other New York hospitals. His system joins gymnastic exercises and the concentration exercises of the Indian yogis with scientific massage movements.

The front pages carry maxims and a doctor's endorsement. The human body, one motto runs, is like a chain, only as strong as its weakest link. Dr William Sharpe wrote in March 1920 to recommend the system highly, noting that no apparatus is needed and that the exercises grade themselves to each person's strength. Jensen promises a health-giving, vitalizing, beautifying course, and the book stands in the great age of mail-order physical culture.
67419-the-english-home-from-charles-i-to:
Gotch's The English Home from Charles I to George IV traces the house in its building, its furnishing and its gardens. Batsford of London put out the second impression, with corrections, in April 1919, a year after the first. Upwards of 300 plates from photographs, drawings and engravings carry the argument.

The frontispiece shows York Buildings and the Adelphi stairs and waterworks, from a water-colour by Thomas Sandby. Gotch had already written on the Renaissance house in England and on the growth of the English house, and here he carries that story to the start of the nineteenth century. A long list of subscribers, headed by the Queen, fills the opening pages.
70114-the-big-four:
Agatha Christie wrote this detective novel, copyright 1927 by Dodd Mead. Dell reprinted the book in New York in June 1972. Contents open with an unexpected guest and a man from the asylum. Li Chang Yen looms behind the plot from chapter three.

A leg of mutton proves key, and a scientist vanishes next. Radium thieves, a house of the enemy, and Croftlands follow fast. A chess problem, a baited trap, and a peroxide blonde appear. A dying Chinaman and the Felsenlabyrinth mark the closing chapters here. A terrible catastrophe and Number Four winning a trick mark the tale near its close.
70384-arthur:
Laurence Binyon's Arthur, a tragedy, was published by Small, Maynard and Company at Boston with a 1923 copyright. Binyon dedicates the play to Sir John and Lady Martin Harvey, and his dedication recalls the June day when he undertook to write for them a play out of Malory's pages.

The cast lists King Arthur, Sir Launcelot, Sir Gawaine and his brothers, Sir Mordred, Queen Guenevere, and Elaine. The first scene opens at Sir Bernard's castle at Astolat, where Lavaine brings word that the king has returned victorious from the north. Launcelot, the herald says, vanished three months ago, and the king means to search the land for his friend.
71726-my-three-years-in-manipur:
Ethel Grimwood wrote My Three Years in Manipur, a memoir printed in London in 1891, with pictures and a plan. Her husband had been offered the post of Political Agent at Manipur, a state on the edge of British India. The book tells of their life there and of their escape from a sudden mutiny.

Early chapters describe the long journey in, the hill tribes such as the Kukis, and the rest houses on the road. At the Residency she writes of the Maharajah, his brother, polo with the princes, and the strange pets they kept. Gardens, language lessons, and visits fill the calm years. Then the rising comes, and the escape gives the book its lasting fame.
73131-unhuman-tour:
Unhuman Tour, in Japanese Kusamakura, is a novel by Soseki Natsume in the Masterpieces of Contemporary Japanese Fiction series. Kazutomo Takahashi translated it for the Japan Times. Thirteen chapters follow an introduction and preface.

Chapter one climbs a mountain into a train of thought. Work with your brains, the narrator muses, and you are liable to be harsh; drift in sentiment, and you may be carried away. This disagreeable human world is the making neither of God nor of the Devil but of common mortals, the neighbours on right and left. When you awake to the truth that moving will not mend it, poetry is born and art creates. The poet and the painter, he says, hold a heaven ordained mission: to rub the sharp corners off disagreeableness so that life, for a brief while, passes pleasantly.
73712-through-bosnia-and-the-herzego-vin: Through Bosnia and the Herzegovina on Foot tells of a walking trip through two rough provinces of the Turkish borderlands while a rising was in progress. The title alone fixes the manner of the trip: no carriage, no train, but the traveler's own feet, day by day, through a land in revolt. Books of this kind sold on the promise of ground seen close and people met on the road. Readers who like hard travel in tense times get a foot tour of the Balkans of the Eastern Question years.
74050-the-prem-sagur:
Captain W Hollings of the forty-seventh regiment of Bengal Native Infantry turned the Prem Sagur into English at Calcutta in 1848. The Military Orphan Press printed the version. Long notes at the front explain his spelling of Hindi words for English readers.

Readers learn that Shree Krishnù Chund is Sri Krishna Chand, and Hustinapoor is Hastinapur. A glossary defines terms such as bhang, ghaut, jogee, and the coss, a measure of distance. Notes cover caste names, the Holi festival powder, and the sixty-four gharis of the Indian day. The tale itself tells the life of Krishna in the popular Hindi form. Hollings keeps brief notes in brackets inside the text.
7425-the-louisa-alcott-reader-a-suppleme:
Louisa M. Alcott's stories were a staple of American schoolrooms, and this reader gathers them for the fourth year of school. Its contents run from A Christmas Dream and The Candy Country to Naughty Jocko, The Skipping Shoes, and Rosy's Journey. How They Ran Away, The Fairy Box, and The Piggy Girl complete a set chosen for young readers.

The opening story sets the pattern: a discontented girl, tired of Christmas and its same old surprises, learns what the holiday can still mean. Alcott's tales mix fantasy with home lessons, always in plain, warm language a child can read aloud. As a school reader, the book was meant to teach reading through delight, and it still works that way.
75036-the-ways-of-the-hour:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote this tale, The Ways of the Hour, late in his long career. Appleton printed this copy in New York in 1892, from plates first set in 1861. Cooper says in his preface what the book is for, in plain terms.

He aims to draw the eye to social ills of the hour. Chief among them, he names the way crime is tried and judged in America. A plate at the front shows a theft, and a talk through a grate, like a novice in a convent, hints at prison scenes. The story form lets Cooper press a grave charge: that the courts of his day too often failed the cause of right.
75768-alexander-balfour:
Alexander Balfour is a memoir of the Liverpool merchant and philanthropist by R H Lundie. James Nisbet and Company of London with Philip, Son and Nephew of Liverpool issued this fifth edition in 1890. Lundie warns that Balfour left few letters to speak for him, being brief and business-like even in good works.

The chapters follow the deeds instead: parentage and boyhood, early Liverpool life, and the Christian merchant. Long sections trace his footsteps among seamen, his seat on the council of education, and home life at Mount Alyn. Conflict follows over the license laws, first in administration and then in legislation. Journeys to Valparaiso and Palestine and jottings from his journals precede the closing days. A funeral sermon and a letter of counsel to young partners in business close the volume.
76216-from-the-yalu-to-port-arthur:
From the Yalu to Port Arthur, a personal record by William Maxwell, was printed by Hutchinson in London in 1906, with 33 illustrations and 3 maps. Maxwell had been special correspondent of the Standard and was lately of the Daily Mail. A prefatory note makes his claim: very few European or American correspondents accompanied the Japanese army. He was the only one with General Kuroki from the Yalu to the Sha ho.

With his interpreter Ito, he says, he was the only outside observer at those engagements and at the last assaults on Port Arthur and its surrender. Chapter summaries trace the war from its origin: the diplomatic struggle over Korea, and Russia's use of Port Arthur. A remarkable confidential Japanese study of the Russian army judged its officers incapable and Kuropatkin not to be feared. The landing in Korea and the entry into Seoul follow.
76422-the-symbolism-of-colour:
Ellen Conroy wrote this study of what colours mean, and how men have read them. A word from Job heads it: speak to the earth and it shall teach you. Her degree stands on the title page, a mark of the book's learned plan.

Colour, for Conroy, is a language older than words. Red, blue, gold, and the rest carry set senses in faith, art, and rite. Her pages trace those senses through church glass, flags, gems, and dress. The tables in the book, she warns, show best in even type. A work of the great age of symbol studies, it fits the time when men read signs in all things. The plain text keeps her charts and notes in place.
76939-the-laws-of-contrast-of-colour:
The Laws of Contrast of Colour, by M E Chevreul, sets out the law of simultaneous contrast and its uses across the arts. John Spanton translated the work from the French, and Routledge, Warne, and Routledge of London issued this new edition in 1861, with illustrations printed in colours. Chevreul directed the dye works of the Gobelins, the great French tapestry manufactory, and his law grew out of its dyeing problems.

The full title lists the trades addressed: painting, decoration of buildings, mosaic work, tapestry and carpet weaving, calico-printing, dress, paper-staining, printing, and military clothing. Illumination, landscape, and flower gardening follow. The chapters proceed by experiment, showing how colours change one another when laid side by side, against black, grey, and their own kin. Chevreul's contrast law shaped both factory practice and the painters who followed.
77432-desolate-splendour:
Michael Sadleir's Desolate Splendour was published by the Macmillan Company of Canada at Toronto in 1923. The dedication page calls it a flamboyant tale. It promises ambitious hedonism, the desolate splendour of a girl's devotion, perverted cruelty, lust for property, and the genial obtuseness of the upright. Eighteen chapters move from Plethern of Morvane through Rockarvon, Viola, Daniel, and the Grays of Clonsall, to London pleasures, a painted earl, sacrifice, and a night at Morvane.

The opening describes the Morvane avenue: wrought-iron gates crowning a hill crest, fencing off a space of sky, with no carriageway beyond them. The new road has left the old approach grass-grown and abandoned to wild flowers and bees. Across the lane the ground falls to the deep, secret valley of Rockarvon. Sadleir's prose is lush and deliberate, a period piece of country-house passion and decay.
77884-the-pacific-coast-scenic-tour:
The Pacific Coast Scenic Tour carries the reader from southern California to Alaska, taking in the Canadian Pacific Railway, Yellowstone Park, and the Grand Canon. Henry Finck wrote it, and Sampson Low printed it in London in 1891. Mount Hood stands among its illustrations.

Finck's preface complains that books on California and Alaska abound, while Oregon and Washington have been comparatively neglected. His tour runs the whole coast from San Diego to Sitka, choosing a few typical places in each state rather than pretending to exhaust the ground. He confesses his love plainly. Eleven years lived on the Pacific side against twelve on the Atlantic taught him that scenery there is grander and climate more delightful. Climate and scenery, in his view, make fully half of human happiness.
78388-a-secret-agent-in-port-arthur:
William Greener published A Secret Agent in Port Arthur in London in 1905, with a facsimile of the author's instructions as a frontispiece. His prefatory note says no eyewitness of the fighting between Russians and Japanese need apologise for a truthful account. Very little, he notes, was actually seen by newspaper correspondents.

Greener makes no claim to a detailed story of the siege. He gives his own experiences in Port Arthur and elsewhere in Manchuria, what he saw, what he was told, and what he thought. His hope is to make readers think about British and American policy in the Far East. Readers get a spy's memoir from the Russo-Japanese War.
794-the-wouldbegoods-being-the-further-a:
E. Nesbit brought back the Bastable children in this sequel to The Treasure Seekers, now bent on being good. Their would-be good deeds go gloriously wrong, from jungle games to a tower of mystery, a circus, and a high-born babe in need of care. Each chapter turns a kind plan into comic chaos.

Oswald and his siblings mean well, and their blunders teach them patience and sense. Nesbit's voice is warm, funny, and true to childhood, and the tales have delighted readers for generations. The book stands with its predecessor as a classic of family adventure, where goodness is learned by trial and error.
8193-the-sceptics-of-the-old-testament-j:
E. J. Dillon, late professor of comparative philology at Kharkoff and doctor of oriental languages at Louvain, presented Job, Koheleth, and Agur as the sceptics of the Old Testament. With English text translated for the first time from the primitive Hebrew as restored on recent philological discoveries. Dedicated to Alexander Vassilyevitch Paschkoff, the volume argues that these three books voice doubt and questioning within Scripture itself.

Dillon's restoration claims to recover an earlier Hebrew text, and his translations aim to let Job's protests, Ecclesiastes' vanity, and Agur's riddles speak freshly. Scholars debate his reconstructions, but the book's thesis endures: the Bible contains its own sceptics. For biblical students, it is a bold, learned attempt to hear doubt as part of faith.
8497-the-poems-and-prose-of-ernest-dowso:
Arthur Symons wrote the memoir that opens this collection of Ernest Dowson's poems and prose, and the contents that follow show why Dowson mattered. Poems include Nuns of the Perpetual Adoration, Villanelle of Sunset, and To One in Bedlam. Amor Umbratilis and Non sum qualis eram bonae sub regno Cynarae follow, the famous lament for Cynara, with prose pieces after.

Dowson, a poet of the decadent nineties, died young, and Symons's memoir frames his brief, troubled life. Readers meet the lyric voice of the Yellow Book era: musical, melancholy, and haunted by lost love. The volume remains the standard introduction to Dowson, through a friend who knew him well.
9098-tacitus-and-bracciolini-the-annals-:
John Wilson Ross wrote this bold attack on a classic text, first published without his name in 1878. He argues that the Annals of Tacitus, the Roman historian, were forged in the fifteenth century by Poggio Bracciolini, a humanist famed for finding old manuscripts. Ross calls the case a question against all received tradition.

Latin quotes from scholars of the day back his charge, and he stresses Bracciolini's skill at imitation. Most scholars reject the claim today, yet the book fascinates. It shows how far doubt about ancient texts can run, and why proof matters in history.
9470-his-hour:
Elinor Glyn, famed for Three Weeks, wrote His Hour in 1910, a romance of Russian high society. The book is called When the Hour Came in England and Russia. Glyn dedicated it to the Grand Duchess Vladimir, who aided her study of Russian character and heard the tale read aloud. A prince named Milaslavski stands at the heart of the story, seen first at a fancy ball in the Winter Palace.

The novel moves through balls, palaces, and proud hearts, as love tests rank and duty in imperial Russia. Glyn writes with lush, frank feeling, and a keen eye for dress, manners, and power. A reader gets a vivid, old-style romance of a vanished court, told by a writer who knew its rooms first hand.
952-tom-swift-and-his-air-glider-or-seek:
A breakdown and a daring project start this Tom Swift tale by Victor Appleton, in which Tom seeks a platinum treasure in Russia. The hand of the Czar, a clue from Russia, and the rescue of Mr. Petrofsky lead to the building of an air glider, a craft that can ride the winds where engines fail.

In a great gale and a storm at sea, spies dog the party, and the airship carries them toward the treasure. Appleton mixes Russian intrigue with aeronautical daring, and Tom's cool head saves the day. The book is a brisk Tom Swift adventure, where a glider, not a gun, wins the prize.
a-reply-to-dr-lightfoot-s-essays-by-the-: Walter Richard Cassels answers Doctor Lightfoot's essays in this reply, first published anonymously in 1889 by the author of Supernatural Religion. He rejoices at Lightfoot's recovery from illness and praises the vigorous preface to the republished essays, while disputing their case for the church. The introduction defends his own volumes against what he calls an error of judgment and temper in rescuing only the most serious part of the reply.
american-scenes-and-christian-slavery-a-: Ebenezer Davies, late minister of Mission Chapel in New Amsterdam, Berbice, tours four thousand miles in the United States and records American scenes and Christian slavery. Writing in 1849, he describes towns, churches, and the slave system he saw, judging American practice by Christian standards. The book is a British visitor's frank report on a divided nation.
at-home-and-abroad-or-things-and-thought:
Margaret Fuller Ossoli's travel writing fills this volume, edited after her death by her brother Arthur B. Fuller. The new and complete edition of 1869 joins her American journeys with her letters from Europe. Fuller, author of Woman in the Nineteenth Century, travelled as the Tribune's correspondent and reported what she saw with a reformer's eye.

Early pages cross lakes and prairies, sorting travellers into those who truly see and those who pass blind. European letters then follow her through Britain and France into Italy. Excitement there runs high: a supposed Austrian spy assassinated at Ferrara, troops marched in, and conspiracy rumours in Rome. Sharp observation and sympathy for Italian freedom give these dispatches their lasting force.
britannica-1911-aberdour:
Aberdour receives a village entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The Fife village on the Firth of Forth shore draws crowds for fine sea-bathing, reached by rail from Edinburgh or steamer from Leith. A ruined castle and a decayed church with Norman work mark its past.

Donibristle House, three miles south-west, seats the earl of Moray and recalls the 1592 murder of the second earl there. Inchcolm island in the parish carries Columba's name and a stone-roofed oratory held for a hermit's cell. Alexander the First founded its Augustinian monastery in 1123, and tower, church, and cloisters stand well kept. Island raids and a Stuart marriage to the Moray line close the island tale.
britannica-1911-aikin-arthur:
Arthur Aikin (1773–1854) built a career that joined chemistry, minerals, and learned societies. Born at Warrington in Lancashire, he learned chemistry from Priestley and cared most for its practical uses. Mineral study pulled him too, and for a short spell in early life he served as a Unitarian minister.

London's Geological Society owed part of its start to Aikin in 1807, and he served as its honorary secretary from 1812 to 1817. His papers for the society dealt with the Wrekin and the coalfield of Shropshire. He later acted as secretary of the Society of Arts and, from 1841, as treasurer of the Chemical Society. His books range from a North Wales tour to a manual of mineralogy and a two-volume dictionary of chemistry and mineralogy, written with his brother. He died in London, valued for sound judgement and broad knowledge.
britannica-1911-arbour:
Arbour, or arbor, names a shady garden bower. Interlaced trees form its covering. Climbing plants on lattice-work form it too. The word originally meant something else entirely. Herber or erber stood behind it. Old French herbier meant a herb collection. Latin herbarium lies behind that form. Pronunciation turned the spelling toward arber. Derby shows the same spelling shift.

Confusion with Latin arbor helped too. Arbor means tree in Latin. By the sixteenth century arbour was standard spelling. Meaning shifted from ground to covering. The proper sense was grass-covered ground. A lawn, herb-garden, or orchard qualified. Usage transferred the name overhead instead. A separate word arbor means a wheel spindle. Clock-making uses that sense particularly.
britannica-1911-arms-and-armour:
Arms and Armour, in the 1911 Britannica, is a vast survey entry on weapons of attack and gear of defence. The oldest weapons found in caves and tombs are prime proof for the story of early man. From their stuff and shape, scholars built the classes and dates of prehistoric life.

The entry sorts attack weapons by the blow they deal and how they are used. Hand arms at close range cleave, crush, thrust, or cut, from axes and clubs to swords and spears. Missile arms, such as darts and javelins, are thrown to shun close fight. A third class shoots its missiles, from bows and catapults to firearms. Side arms worn at the belt and small arms get their own place in the scheme. Defence gear is then set out as body armour, head and limb guards, and shields of many kinds.
britannica-1911-bahawalpur:
Bahawalpur is a native state of India within the Punjab. It stretches over 300 miles along the left bank of the Sutlej, the Punjnud, and the Indus. The Rajputana desert lies to its south. It is the chief Mahommedan state in the Punjab, covering 15,918 square miles with 720,877 people in 1901.

The land is remarkably level: a fertile river strip about ten miles broad, then desert where travellers sink in loose sand and wells run a hundred feet deep. Its nawab comes of the Daudputra family. That family claims descent from the Prophet's uncle. He made his house independent of the Afghans in the late 1700s. He has kept loyal to an 1838 treaty with the British. Canal watering from the 1870s doubled the revenue.
britannica-1911-baikie-william-balfour:
Baikie, William Balfour (1824-1864), was a Scottish explorer, naturalist, and student of languages born at Kirkwall in Orkney, son of a naval captain. He studied medicine at Edinburgh, took his degree, and joined the royal navy in 1848, soon catching Sir Roderick Murchison's notice.

In 1854 Baikie sailed as surgeon and naturalist on a Niger expedition. Its commander died on the way. Baikie took charge of the party. He ran the steamer Pleiad 250 miles up the Benue. That was beyond all earlier explorers. The voyage lasted 118 days without losing a man. A second expedition wrecked in rapids. Baikie stayed on alone regardless. He bought the site of Lokoja, where the Niger and Benue meet. He made treaty with the Fula emir. Then he began building a future city there.
britannica-1911-bajour:
Bajour, or Bajaur, is a small district in India's North-West Frontier Province. Pathan races of Afghan origin people it. The district runs 45 miles by 20. It lies high east of the Kunar valley. Rugged hills wall it off from Kunar. The old Kabul to India road crossed there.

Tarkani Pathans form nearly the whole population. Their clans include Mamunds and Isazai. Together they number about 100,000 people. Mohmand hills lie to the south. Swat lies east across the Panjkora. Dir lies north beyond a watershed. All drainage flows east to the Panjkora. Nawagai is the chief town. Its khan guards the Chitral road for Britain. Umra Khan of Jandol once threatened the whole region. His ambition helped bring the 1893 boundary settlement. His Chitral invasion followed in 1895.
britannica-1911-balrampur:
Balrampur was a town of British India near the river Rapti, in the Gonda district of the United Provinces. It stood 28 miles from Gonda and held 16,723 people in 1901. The town lends its name to one of the largest talukdari estates in the province, held by great landlords under the local system.

Its raja, Sir Drigbijai Singh, stayed conspicuously loyal during the Mutiny and was rewarded with more land and lasting privileges. His death in 1882 set off long lawsuits, and the estate fell into chancery. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the estate income as £120,000 and notes schools and hospitals kept up from it, plus a large palace and a handsome modern temple in the town.
britannica-1911-bampur:
Bampur is a town of Persia in the province of Baluchistan, 330 miles south-east of Kerman, at 1,720 feet above the sea. Its population was about 2,000. It serves as capital of the province and stands on the Bampur river, which flows west and ends in a salt depression called Jaz-morian.

The old citadel, on a rise north of the river, had fallen wholly to ruin. A new fort, Kalah Nasseri, rose in the 1880s at Fahraj, fifteen miles east, and Fahraj grew past Bampur in size. The 1911 Britannica entry adds a scholarly puzzle: some identify Fahraj with Poura, where Alexander the Great halted on his march from India, while others favour Bampur itself.
britannica-1911-barfleur:
Barfleur is a small seaport of north-western France, overlooking the Bay of the Seine, in the department of Manche. It lies about 22 miles north-east of Valognes by rail, and its population in 1906 was 1,069. In the middle ages it ranked among the chief ports of embarkation for England.

One wreck gives the entry its lasting note. In 1120 the White Ship, carrying Prince William, the only son of Henry I of England, went down outside the harbour. About two miles north stands Cape Barfleur, with a lighthouse 233 feet high. The 1911 Britannica entry is short, keeping to the port's place, its medieval role, the wreck, and the cape.
britannica-1911-barrackpur:
Barrackpur is a town and magisterial subdivision of British India, in the Twenty-four Parganas district of Bengal. It is the largest cantonment, or military station, in Lower Bengal, with room for two batteries of artillery, the wing of a European regiment, and two native battalions. Troops have been stationed there since 1772, which is said to explain its name.

Job Charnock, the founder of Calcutta, built a bungalow and set up a small bazaar here as early as 1689. The cantonment stands on the left bank of the Hugli, with its bazaar, tanks, and parade ground. South of it lies the park laid out by Lord Wellesley, holding Government House and Lady Canning's tomb. The 1911 Britannica entry recalls the town's part in the sepoy mutinies of 1824 and 1857.
britannica-1911-bellecour:
Bellecour (1725–1778) was a French actor, born Jean Claude Gilles Colson, son of a portrait painter. Art tempted him first, but he left the brush for the stage and played in the provinces. The Comédie Française called him in 1750, yet his first night as Achilles in Iphigénie fell flat.

Comedy suited Bellecour better, and he filled its parts with credit for thirty years. A natural player, he gladly let fellow actors shine, which made him well liked. He wrote a successful play, Fausses apparences, and helped the theatre by editing other men’s work. His wife, acting as Madame Bellecour, won fame in Molière’s soubrette parts before dying poor in 1799.
britannica-1911-bhagalpur:
Bhagalpur is a city of British India, in the Behar province of Bengal, described in this 1911 Britannica article. It stands on the right bank of the Ganges, 265 miles from Calcutta, on the East Indian railway, and had 75,760 people in 1901. Its chief school is the Tejnarayan Jubilee college, founded in 1887 and kept up almost wholly by fees.

The article then turns to the district of the same name, which stretches across both banks of the Ganges over 4,226 square miles. More than two million people lived there in 1901. South of the river, hill ranges and highlands give fine scenery, with gorges, ravines, and rich forest. The lowlands are fertile, well watered, and highly farmed. North of the Ganges the land is level, yet varied with trees and green growth.
britannica-1911-bharatpur:
Bharatpur, also spelled Bhurtpore, is a native state of India in the Rajputana agency, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a geography and history entry. Its area covers a little under two thousand square miles. The country is generally level, about seven hundred feet above the sea, with small detached hills that hold good building stone and, in some, iron ore.

One river, the Banganga, flows through the state. It rises in Jaipur territory, passes through the heart of Bharatpur, and joins the Jamna below Agra. The state rose to importance under Suraj Mall, who played a conspicuous part in the destruction of the Delhi empire. He built the forts of Dig and Kumbher in 1730 and received the title of raja in 1756. He then joined the great Mahratta army with thirty thousand troops, but he left the confederacy in time to escape the murderous defeat at Panipat.
britannica-1911-bijapur:
Bijapur is an ancient city and modern district in the southern division of Bombay, India. It stands on the Southern Mahratta railway, 60 miles south of Sholapur. Its 1901 population was 23,811. The city was once the splendid capital of an independent state of the same name. Now it holds only traces of that grandeur. The 1911 Britannica entry calls it the most picturesque collection of ruins in India.

Yusuf Adil Shah, founder of the state, raised the city to greatness. The citadel he built runs a mile around, ringed by a ditch 100 yards wide. Old Hindu temple remains stand inside it. An underground water system of reservoirs and aqueducts once served the city. The district grows millet, wheat, pulse, oil-seeds, and cotton. Famine struck hard in 1876 to 1878 and again in 1899 to 1900.
britannica-1911-bilaspur:
Bilaspur is a town and district of British India in the Central Provinces. The town stands on the right bank of the river Arpa. Tradition says a fisherwoman named Bilasa founded it in the 17th century. It rose to note only after the Mahratta invasion of 1741. A Mahratta official then settled there and began a fort, never finished. In 1901 the town held 18,937 people. It is a key junction on the Bengal-Nagpur railway.

The district covers 7,602 square miles in the upper Mahanadi basin. Hill ranges enclose it on the north, west, and east. The south lies open, well farmed, and thick with villages in fruit groves. The 1911 Britannica entry traces its rajas back through thirty-six forts and fifty-five kings. The Mahrattas seized the country without a struggle in 1741. In 1854 it lapsed finally to the British government.
britannica-1911-bonheur-du-jour:
Bonheur du jour is the name of a lady's small writing desk that came into French fashion about 1760 and caught on at once. The entry is a short piece of furniture history. The desk is always light and graceful in build, whatever details a maker chose.

Its mark is a raised back, which may hold a tiny cabinet, a nest of drawers, or only a mirror. The top is often ringed by a chased, gilded bronze rail and used to set out small ornaments. One drawer usually sits under the writing surface. The finest pieces date from the first twenty-five years after its launch. They are inlaid with fine wood pictures, edged with rare woods, mounted in gilt bronze, or panelled with Oriental lacquer.
britannica-1911-bouille-francois-claude-:
François Claude Amour, marquis de Bouillé (1739–1800), was a French general who tried to save Louis XVI from the Revolution. He served in the Seven Years' War, and as a governor in the Antilles he fought the English in the American war. Back in France he governed the Three Bishoprics, Alsace, and Franche-Comté.

At Metz he quarrelled constantly with the town council and crushed army mutinies at Metz and Nancy with brutality. He planned for the king to flee to a frontier town and appeal to foreign nations against the revolutionists. Louis's arrest at Varennes killed the plan. Bouillé then went to Russia to press Catherine II to intervene, and later to England, where he died in 1800 after joining royalist attempts on France. His memoirs of the Revolution appeared in 1801.
britannica-1911-bridgman-frederick-arthu:
Frederick Arthur Bridgman (born 1847) was an American artist born at Tuskegee, Alabama, on 10 November 1847. He began as a draughtsman for the American Bank Note Company in New York in 1864-1865, studying at the Brooklyn Art School and the National Academy of Design in the same years. In 1866 he went to Paris and became a pupil of J. L. Gerome, and Paris stayed his base.

A trip to Egypt in 1873-1874 turned his art toward eastern scenes, which won quick notice. His large Funeral Procession of a Mummy on the Nile, shown at the Paris Salon in 1877 and bought by James Gordon Bennett, brought him the cross of the Legion of Honour. Other named works include An American Circus in Normandy, Procession of the Bull Apis, now at the Corcoran Art Gallery in Washington, and a Rumanian Lady in Philadelphia.
britannica-1911-broke-arthur:
Arthur Broke, also spelt Brooke (died 1563), was an English author who wrote the first English version of the story of Romeo and Juliet. His Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet, printed in 1562, is a rhymed retelling. It was taken not straight from Bandello's novels of 1554 but from the French version by Boaistuau and Belleforest, with some detail of Broke's own added.

That indirect path matters: the poem holds many scenes found nowhere else that Shakespeare later used in Romeo and Juliet. There is no reasonable doubt it stands as the main source of the play. Broke himself perished by shipwreck in 1563, sailing from Newhaven to join English troops fighting on the Huguenot side in France. The entry closes by pointing to an 1875 reprint that sets his poem beside Paynter's prose version for close comparison.
britannica-1911-bucentaur:
The bucentaur, in Italian bucintoro, was the state galley of the doges of Venice, from which, every year on Ascension Day until 1789, they performed the ceremony of wedding the sea. This 1911 Britannica article explains the name as a medieval Latin form of buzino d'oro, “golden bark,” and rejects the fanciful link with a Greek ox-centaur.

The ceremony, called the Marriage of the Adriatic, marked Venice's dominion over the sea and was established about A.D. 1000 after the doge Orseolo II conquered Dalmatia; a procession of boats followed the doge's great galley out through the Lido while prayers were said and holy water cast on the waves. The last and finest bucentaur, built in 1729, was destroyed by the French in 1798 for its golden decorations, and its remains and a model survive at Venice.
britannica-1911-buldur:
Buldur is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Buldur, also spelled Burdur, was the chief town of a district in Asia Minor. Christians of the area called it Polydorion. It stands among gardens at a height of 3150 feet.

The entry is short and gives the plain facts. The town lay about two miles from a brackish lake, the ancient Ascania Limne. Linen weaving and leather tanning were its chief trades. A good carriage road ran to Dineir, and much grain moved along it from the Buldur plain. A railway also linked the town with Dineir and Egirdir. The population is given as 12,000. Readers who meet the name in travel or history writing will find its place and character fixed here in a few lines.
britannica-1911-burhanpur:
Burhanpur is a town of British India in the Central Provinces, on the north bank of the Tapti river. It stands three hundred ten miles north east of Bombay, near a rail station. The town was founded in the year fourteen hundred by a prince of Khandesh. His heirs held it for two hundred years, until Akbar took their kingdom. It then formed the chief seat of Mogul rule in the Deccan.

Shah Jahan moved the Deccan capital to Aurangabad in sixteen thirty five. The Mahrattas plundered Burhanpur in sixteen eighty five, and battles were fought near it for years. In seventeen sixty the town was ceded to the peshwa, who passed it to Sindhia. British forces under Wellesley took it in eighteen o three. A treaty that same year gave it back to Sindhia. It passed to British rule at last in eighteen sixty.
britannica-1911-cavour:
Cavour is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of Piedmont, Italy, in the province of Turin. It stands 32 miles south west of Turin by rail and steam tram, by way of Pinerolo. The town counted 2091 people in 1901. Its commune counted 6843. It lies on the north side of a huge isolated mass of granite, the Rocca di Cavour, which rises from the plain. A Roman village stood on the summit.

The ancient town was called Caburrum or Forum Vibii. It belonged to the province of the Alpes Cottiae. Some ruins of medieval fortifications remain. The town gave its name to the Benso family of Chieri. That family was raised to the marquisate in 1771. The statesman Cavour was a member of it. The entry is short and closes with a reference to Mommsen on the ancient name. Place, rock, and family name are its whole content.
britannica-1911-chauffeur:
Chauffeur is a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French word, from chauffer, to heat. In French the term first named a man in charge of a forge or a furnace. From that sense it passed to the stoker on a locomotive or in a steamship. The man who fed the fire held the name in each setting.

In its anglicised sense the word has narrowed. It now belongs in particular to the professional driver of a motor vehicle. The entry marks the shift in a few lines, from forge to footplate to motor car. It also points the reader to the article on Brigandage for another old French use of the word. A single heating root thus ends by naming the paid driver of the newest machine on the road.
britannica-1911-chota-nagpur:
Chota Nagpur, a division of British India in Bengal, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It consists of five British districts and two feudatory states. The land is a hilly, forest-clad plateau between the basins of the Sone, the Ganges, and the Mahanadi. Its people are mostly of aboriginal races. The British districts cover 27,101 square miles. Their population in 1901 was 4,900,429.

The plateau is an offshoot of the Vindhyan range, with a mean height above 2,000 feet. It is the source of many rivers, among them the Damodar and the Brahmani. Sal forests abound. Jungle products include timber, lac, tussur silk, and mahua flowers. Coal exists in large quantities, and the chief workings at Jherria began in 1893.
britannica-1911-collier-arthur:
Arthur Collier (1680–1732) was an English thinker, born at the rectory of Steeple Langford in Wiltshire. He was born on 12 October 1680 and entered Pembroke College, Oxford, in 1697. In 1698 he and his brother William moved to Balliol. His father died in 1697, and it was set that the family living of Langford Magna should go to Arthur when he was old enough. He was given that post in 1704 and held it till his death.

Collier's sermons show no trace of his bold thoughts on faith. He seems to have been true in the work of his post. He was often in want of money, and at last he had to sell the rights to the Langford post to Corpus Christi College to free himself. His views on thought grew out of a close study of Descartes and Malebranche.
britannica-1911-conway-henry-seymour:
Henry Seymour Conway (1721-1795) was an English field marshal and statesman. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica presents him as cousin and close friend of Horace Walpole. He sat in both Irish and English parliaments for over forty years. Army service abroad ran beside that long public career from youth.

He fought at Fontenoy and held a regiment at Culloden in turn. A failed attack on Rochefort in 1757 hurt his standing for a time. Later German campaigns under Prince Ferdinand restored his name in arms. In parliament he spoke against general warrants in the Wilkes case. The king stripped his posts for that stand, sparking a fresh dispute.
britannica-1911-decatur:
Decatur is a city article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Decatur is a city in Illinois, the county seat of Macon county. It stands near the Sangamon River, east of Springfield. Its growth was swift: from 16,841 people in 1890 to 31,140 in 1910.

Four railways served the city, and the Wabash kept its car shops there. Electric lines of the Illinois Traction System tied it to many nearby cities. The entry names three large parks and a public library. James Millikin University, founded in 1901, stood by Fairview Park on a campus of thirty-five acres. The university ran schools of liberal arts and engineering, among others. It also taught domestic economy, fine arts, and commerce. The article gives a full picture of a young industrial city built on rails and schooling.
britannica-1911-ellichpur:
Ellichpur, or Illichpur, is a town of India in the Amraoti district of Berar, with a population of 26,082 in 1901. The town is first mentioned with certainty in the 13th century as one of the famous cities of the Deccan. Though tributary to the Mahommedans after 1294, it stayed under Hindu rule until 1318. It then came directly under Mahommedan rule.

Ellichpur was at intervals the capital of the province of Berar until the Mogul occupation moved the governor's seat to Balapur. The town keeps many relics of the nawabs of Berar. It has ginning factories and a large trade in cotton and forest produce, and good roads link it with Amraoti and Chikalda. The former district of Ellichpur, 2605 square miles with 297,403 people in 1901, was merged into Amraoti district in 1905. The civil station of Paratwada, two miles away, holds the main public buildings.
britannica-1911-emmett-daniel-decatur:
Emmett, Daniel Decatur (1815–1904), was an American songwriter born at Mount Vernon, Ohio. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry for him is short, only a short paragraph, and it rests on two claims to notice. He started the “negro minstrel” performances that became so popular in America and England from 1842 onward. He also composed a number of songs that had a great vogue for a time.

One song outlasted that vogue. Emmett is remembered above all as the writer of the famous Southern war-song “Dixie,” which he composed in 1859. The entry gives no account of his later life beyond his death year, 1904. A reader gets a brief record of a man whose fame narrowed to one tune. That tune, written before the war it came to stand for, carried his name far beyond the theatres where his other songs were sung and forgotten.
britannica-1911-exequatur:
An exequatur is the letter patent by which a sovereign guarantees a foreign consul his office's rights and privileges. A foreign office issues it, and the sovereign signs it. It secures the consul's recognition in the state where he will serve. A consul not appointed by commission receives no exequatur. In that case a notice in the Gazette must suffice instead. The document can in principle be withdrawn.

In practice, the entry says, withdrawal is avoided. Where a consul gives offence, his government gets the chance to recall him first. The notice is a short legal dictionary entry of a few lines. It fixes the term by its source, its signer and its effect. It also quietly marks the courtesy that governs how consuls are removed. Nothing more is claimed for the word than this formal warrant of recognition.
britannica-1911-faridpur:
Faridpur is a town and district of British India in the Dacca division of eastern Bengal and Assam. The town stands on an old channel of the Ganges and had 11,649 people in 1901. It has a Baptist mission and a government high school. The district covers 2,281 square miles of flat delta land. The north is higher and sandy; the south sinks into one great swamp. At flood height nearly the whole district lies under water.

Villages stand on raised ground along the delta streams, strung unbroken for miles. Lagoons between them slowly silt up. Rain averages 66 inches a year, and mean temperature 76.9 degrees. The Ganges, locally the Padma, meets the Jamuna at Goalanda, and large cargo boats use it all year. Rice is the great crop. District population in 1901 was 1,937,646, up 6 per cent in the decade, and most trade moves by river.
britannica-1911-fatehpur:
Fatehpur, also spelled Fathipur or Futtehpoor, is a town and district of British India in the Allahabad division of the United Provinces. The town lies 73 miles by rail north-west of Allahabad and had 19,281 people in 1901. The district covers 1,618 square miles in the south-eastern corner of the Doab, the land between the Ganges and the Jumna, which bound it north and south.

The district is an alluvial plain built by the two rivers, level and well cultivated in the centre, cut by ravines near the banks. Its history runs from a Pathan conquest in 1194 through Mogul, Mahratta and Oudh rule to cession to the East India Company in 1801. It rose in rebellion in June 1857. Its 1901 population was 686,391.
britannica-1911-ghazipur:
Ghazipur is a place article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town and district of British India. The town stands on the left bank of the Ganges, forty-four miles east of Benares. It is the head office of the government opium department. All opium from the United Provinces is gathered and made there under a monopoly.

The town also has scent works that use the roses grown round it. Lord Cornwallis, governor-general of India, died at Ghazipur in 1805. A domed monument and a marble statue by Flaxman stand over his grave. The count of 1901 gave the town 39,429 people. The district covers 1,389 square miles of the flat Ganges plain. The river splits it into two unequal parts, with no hills in either.
britannica-1911-giaour: Giaour is a word Turks used for people who are not Muslims, with Christians meant above all. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces it through Turkish from a Persian word for an unbeliever. First used as a term of scorn, it grew so common that in most use no insult is meant. The entry compares it to a like term in China and to the Arabic word kaffir, which also passed into wide use as a plain name.
britannica-1911-giry-arthur:
Arthur Giry (1848-1899) was a French historian, born at Trevoux on 29 February 1848. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him through the lycee at Chartres, a spell in administration and journalism, and then the Ecole des Chartes. There, under J. Quicherat, he found his bent for the middle ages.

He began with the municipal charters of St Omer, and his first large work was a history of that town and its institutions to the 14th century, in 1877. Realizing that one town's charters need comparison with others, he took up the study of town origins where Augustin Thierry had left it. His lectures at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes revived interest in municipal history across France. The entry closes with his later career and death at Paris on 13 November 1899, amid the Zola trial appointments.
britannica-1911-gorakhpur:
Gorakhpur, a city of the United Provinces, is placed in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the left bank of the river Rapti in India. In 1901 its folk came to over sixty-four thousand in count. Men hold it was founded about the year 1400 of our era. It serves as the civil head town of its wide district.

The town is a spread of village sites with farm plots between. Most of its folk work the land for their daily bread. Its district runs to over four thousand square miles of plain. That plain lies just south of the low Himalayan slopes in India. Rivers, lakes, and marshes cut its flat face at close gaps. Dense woods stand thick in its north and centre parts.
britannica-1911-gorgei-arthur:
Arthur Gorgei (1818- ) was a Hungarian soldier, born at Toporcz in Upper Hungary on 30 January 1818. The 1911 Britannica entry makes him of a Saxon noble family turned Protestant. He entered the Bodyguard of Hungarian Nobles at Vienna in 1837, mixing service with university study, then left the army in 1845 to study chemistry at Prague.

When revolution broke out in 1848 he offered his sword to the Hungarian government. Rising fast in the Honved army, he blocked the Croatians at the Danube and won at Ozora, where 10,000 prisoners fell to him. The entry also records the hanging of Count Eugene Zichy after a court-martial. Made commander of the army of the Upper Danube, he chose retreat before Windischgratz against Kossuth's protests. The long article follows his generalship through the war of independence and its bitter end.
britannica-1911-haden-sir-francis-seymou:
Sir Francis Seymour Haden (1818–1910) was an English surgeon and etcher. He was born in London on 16 September 1818. His father was a well-known doctor and music lover. Haden studied at University College, London, and at the Sorbonne. He joined the College of Surgeons in 1842. Surgery gave him a busy, distinguished career. Etching gave him a second one.

He became the foremost British exponent of original etching. He was the principal cause of its revival in England. In 1880 he founded the Royal Society of Painter-Etchers. He ruled it as president with a strong hand. He taught himself from old dealers' portfolios. Dürer, Lucas van Leyden and Rembrandt were his masters. His monograph separated Rembrandt's true etchings from false ones. He was knighted in 1894. Whistler was his brother-in-law.
britannica-1911-hajipur:
Hajipur, a town of British India in Bengal, is the subject of a brief place note in the 1911 Britannica. It stands on the Gandak River just where that stream meets the Ganges. The town of Patna lies across the great river from its banks. Its folk count for nineteen oh one was twenty one thousand three hundred ninety eight. Rail tracks of the Bengal line serve the town and its trade.

Wars of Akbar with rebel Afghan chiefs put the town in the tales of the age. Town troops took it by siege twice, in fifteen seventy two and fifteen seventy four. A plain stone mosque stands in the old fort bounds of the town. Trade by water in three ways gives it weight as a mart. That post on two rivers is the root of its trade worth.
britannica-1911-harfleur:
Harfleur is a port of France described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the department of Seine-Inferieure, about six miles east of Havre by rail. Its people numbered 2,864 in 1906. The town sits in the rich valley of the Lezarde, at the foot of wooded hills near the north bank of the Seine mouth.

Sand from its stream had near choked the port. The Tancarville canal of 1887 tied it once more to Havre and to the Seine, and ships of good draft can lie at its quays. It trades in coal and timber and holds a fishery. The church of St Martin, of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, has a tall stone spire that serves as a sea mark. Of the old castle scant ruins stand by a park.
britannica-1911-hastinapur:
Hastinapur is an ancient city of British India in the Meerut district. Its city entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies on the bank of a former bed of the Ganges river. It was the capital of the great Pandava kingdom of old legend.

That kingdom is famed in the Mahabharata, the great national epic poem. Hastinapur may be one of the earliest Aryan towns past the Punjab. Mounds on the site are said to mark the Lunar princes home. After the famed war of the epic, the town stayed a capital for a time. A Ganges flood at last swept it away, and rule moved to Kausambi.
britannica-1911-hesilrige-sir-arthur:
Sir Arthur Hesilrige (d. 1661), second baronet, was an English parliamentarian from Noseley in Leicestershire. A puritan with a dislike of Laud, he sat for Leicestershire in the Short and Long Parliaments of 1640. He took a lead in Strafford's attainder and the Militia Bill. He was one of the five members impeached on the 3rd of January 1642.

In the war he raised a troop of horse for Essex and fought at Edgehill. Under Waller in the West, he led his cuirassiers, the Lobsters, at Lansdown and Roundway Down. When army and parliament split, he backed the army and Cromwell. Under the Self-denying Ordinance he gave up his command and led the Independents in parliament. As governor of Newcastle from December 1647 he held the town and beat the Royalists in 1648. He approved the king's execution but had refused to judge at the trial.
britannica-1911-honfleur:
Honfleur is a seaport of north-western France, in the department of Calvados, 57 m. N.E. of Caen by rail. Its population was 8,735 in 1906. It stands at the foot of a semicircle of hills, on the south shore of the Seine estuary, opposite Havre. Its church of St Catherine is built wholly of timber, in two parallel naves.

St Leonard's church keeps a fine 16th-century portal and rose-window under a later tower. The town holds ruins of a 16th-century castle, the Lieutenance, and a hotel de ville with library and museum. Above it stands the chapel of Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, a sailors' shrine said to have been founded in 1034. The port, sheltered by the Côte de Grâce, joins a tidal harbour to four floating basins, some 27 acres of water in all.
britannica-1911-hoshiarpur:
Hoshiarpur is a town of British India, in the Jullundur division of the Punjab, with 17,549 people in 1901. Tradition gives its founding to the early 14th century. In 1809 Ranjit Singh occupied it, and the maharaja kept a large cantonment a mile south-east of the town. The British held it for some years after annexing the Punjab in 1849. Its trades are cotton goods, inlaid woodwork, lacquered ware, shoes and copper vessels.

Its district covers 2,244 square miles and held 989,782 people in 1901, a fall of 2 per cent in the decade after a rise of 12 per cent before. Hill and plain split it nearly in half. The east face is the westward slope of the Solar Singhi Hills; a lower Siwalik line runs parallel. Between the two chains stretches a valley of uneven width, the Jaswan Dun. The account goes on through the district's rivers, crops and administration.
britannica-1911-hosur: Hosur is a town of British India, in the Salem district of Madras, 24 m. E. of Bangalore. Its population was 6,695 in 1901. It holds an old fort, often named in the history of the Mysore wars, and a fine castellated mansion built by a former collector. Close by stands the remount depot, set up in 1828, where Australian horses are acclimatized and trained for artillery and cavalry use in southern India. The entry is a short gazetteer note.
britannica-1911-jaipur:
Jaipur is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a city and state in India, in the Rajputana agency. The city takes its name from Maharaja Jai Singh the Second, who founded it in 1728. It counts as a new town by Indian standards.

The article praises the plan of the city streets. It is the one city in India laid out in straight blocks. Six equal parts are split by cross streets, and the main streets run 111 feet wide. The houses wear pink plaster in place of sandstone. A great palace stands at the centre, with a noted star watching tower near by. The city held 160,167 people in 1901. The wider state, dry and sandy in the middle, held more than two and a half million.
britannica-1911-jangipur:
Jangipur, also called Jahangirpur, is a town of British India in Bengal. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Bhagirathi river in the Murshidabad district of Bengal. Counts from nineteen o one put its people at just under eleven thousand.

Tradition says the Mogul emperor Jahangir founded the town in past times. In early British rule it was a key centre of the silk trade. An East India Company trade post was based in the town then. Later the town became best known as a toll post on the river. About ten thousand boats are logged there each year for tolls.
britannica-1911-jashpur:
Jashpur, a tributary state of India in the Central Provinces, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was transferred from Bengal in 1905. The country is split almost evenly into high and low lands. The Uparghat plateau in the east rises 2,200 feet above the sea, and its hills reach 3,527 feet at Ranijula.

The only river of note is the Ib, in whose bed diamonds are found. Its sands have been washed for gold from time beyond memory. Jashpur iron, smelted by the Kols, is highly prized in the region. Jungles of sal forest abound and harbour elephant, bison, and other wild beasts. Jungle products sent out include lac, silk cocoons, and beeswax. The entry gives the state an area of 1,948 square miles and 132,114 people in 1901, with a revenue put at eight thousand pounds.
britannica-1911-jodhpur:
Jodhpur, also called Marwar, is a native state of India in the Rajputana agency, covering 34,963 square miles. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its people in 1901 as 1,935,565, a fall of 23 per cent in ten years blamed on famine. The land is a sandy plain split by the river Luni and dotted with cone-shaped hills.

The Luni rises by the sacred lake of Pushkar and runs south-west until it sinks in the marshes at the head of the Runn of Cutch. Its water is mostly salt or brackish, though sweet water is found in wells near its banks. Salt comes from the great lake of Sambhar on the border, and marble is mined in the north. Rathor Rajputs rule, while Marwari traders are found at work across all India.
britannica-1911-johnston-arthur:
Arthur Johnston is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1587, he was a Scottish doctor and a writer of Latin verse. He was the son of a landowner in Aberdeenshire, and on his mother's side a grandson of Lord Forbes.

The article follows his path through schools and courts. He took his medical degree at Padua in 1610 and lived for a time in France. Archbishop Laud backed his verse, in part to dent the fame of Buchanan as a Latin poet. In 1637 he became head of King's College, Aberdeen. His name rests on two books of that year. One is a verse rendering of the Psalms. The other is a store of Latin verse by Scottish poets of his day.
britannica-1911-jones-henry-arthur:
Henry Arthur Jones, an English writer for the stage, gets a life and works list in the 1911 Britannica. Born in Buckinghamshire in eighteen fifty one, he was the son of a farmer. He earned his bread from a young age and wrote in his free hours. His first piece was staged at Exeter when he was twenty seven. Four years on, The Silver King brought him a great hit.
